speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN SPEAKER'S GALLERY OF DELEGATION FROM ALBERTA LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY
speechtext: May I bring to the attention of the House the presence in the Speaker's Gallery of a delegation from the Legislative Assembly of the province of Alberta led by the Assembly's Deputy Speaker, Mr. William Diachuk.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN SPEAKER'S GALLERY OF DELEGATION FROM ALBERTA LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN SPEAKER'S GALLERY OF DELEGATION FROM ALBERTA LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Mr. Diachuk and his five colleagues are in Ottawa participating in a program of parliamentary visits and exchanges between federal and provincial legislatures sponsored by the Canadian branch of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. It will be agreed, I am sure, that these exchange visits will be of benefit to Canadian legislators, to their respective parliaments, and to Canada as a whole. On behalf of all members I extend to our distinguished colleagues from the province of Alberta a most hearty welcome.
[ Translation]
On behalf of all my colleagues in the House of Commons, I wish to call the attention to the presence of our parliamentary colleagues from Alberta and to extend to them a warm welcome both in Ottawa and in our parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Last night I spoke in the House in the debate on the resolution and amendment on bilingualism. In this connection I would like to draw the attention of the House to page 4417 of Hansard and, in particular, to a gross error that appears in paragraph No. 2. Ordinarily I would not rise to correct a printing error in Hansard but because this error is of such a serious nature I am left with absolutely no alternative but to do so on a point of order.
I fully realize that this Hansard error will no doubt please those sitting opposite and I expect that the trained seals will holler as usual.

TABLING OF ANNUAL REPORTS OF AIR CANADA AND CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
speechtext:
I have the honour to table copies, in both official languages, of the annual reports for Air Canada and the Canadian National Railways for the financial year which ended on December 31, 1972.
Mr. Speaker, neither of these reports has been certified by auditors. The auditors' reports will be tabled as soon as the bill on the financing and equity of the Canadian National Railways, which provides for the appointment of auditors, has been adopted. The annual reports are tabled now in order to conform as much as possible to the existing legislation and to give hon. members the opportunity to examine the activities of Air Canada and the Canadian National Railways for 1972.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the rapidly increasing mortgage rates which now have gone up to the disastrous level of 9V4 per cent, and in view of the fact that at this rate a home owner with a 25-year mortgage of $20,000 will pay an outrageous $31,720 in interest charges alone, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Grier):

subsubtopic: FEED GRAIN SUPPLY-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I wish to seek the unanimous consent of the House to discuss such an inportant and urgent matter that we should not run the risk of letting it deteriorate further and impede the Canadian economy.
I refer to the problem of feed grain concerning not only grain producers but also increasing the agricultural producers in eastern Canada.
I move, seconded by the member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin):
That the House adjourn to consider immediately the solutions to the problem of feed grain stocks for eastern producers in order to assure them fair prices and remove that difference of almost $1 per bushel between eastern and western Canada.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certain a lot of people in Canada are very concerned with these regulations and feel that we should get on by negotiating with the civil service associations of Canada-after an election which made a change in the direction-in order to provide some protection for those apparently not able to protect themselves.
Speaking on this subject yesterday, I said that I did not see how we would be able to enact a bill of rights on language and language protection. Since then, I have given some consideration to the type of legislation that we have used on other occasions. I am thinking of the type of legislation that was used when we amended the Criminal Code and a large number of acts in order to include a specific idea in those acts. This bill was put together in a form that would allow the various acts to be opened only for the purpose of providing the protection that was desired. I have also had the opportunity of reading several of the statements issued by the Civil Service Association to the effect that it was not interested in having these regulations put into legislation. The association thought amendments might be needed from time to time and was in the process of negotiating for amendments to the regulations.
If I had not been assured by the then Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, that the terms of these regulations were being provided as a protection for all civil servants, I would not have voted for the Official Languages Act. Those assurances were given by the government of the day. They were given to parliament and I am just as firmly committed to this protection today as I was then. Mr. Speaker, I am not the least bit desirous of having parliament pass what I would consider to be a basic bill of rights for unilingual employees in the civil service, either French or English, or for those bilingual employees, which is going to destroy this protection.
June 5, 1973

I am not sure if the Civil Service Association believes it can negotiate bilingual districts. I am not sure if it thinks it is capable of making the decisions that will be necessary in determining those areas to which this resolution will apply to and those areas to which it will not. I have not found the Civil Service Association to be very strong, Mr. Speaker. I have found civil servants to be passive, to go along with almost anything that was decided as long as they got more money. I have known many civil servants who have fallen into the bad graces of the government. One of these later became a cabinet minister in this House, but he had sat for several years in an office with nothing on his desk because somebody had decided he was "in Coventry" and he just took it. I have not found civil servants to be strong willed, Mr. Speaker, and I do not think they are able to protect themselves. I am not of the opinion that either the Civil Service Association or the civil service is so strong in an advisory sense that they can protect themselves.
I am sure there are going to be amendments and changes; I am sure amendments will have to be negotiated but I am also sure, representing as I do a number of people of both French and English extraction who speak one of the official languages, and in many cases both the official languages, that those people agree with the terms of this resolution. They believe that we should have a bill of rights in respect of language in Canada in order to eliminate many of the problems that have developed over the last few years.
I have heard of very few cases that were pursued to arbitration, even when a person was told that he no longer had a job because it was now classified bilingual and he was not capable of taking bilingual training. I have seen jobs red circled. In many cases I am sure that the person took a position lower than the one to which he was entitled rather than make an issue. I am sure that is true of the association. However, it is possible the association will develop until it reaches a level of competence in the adversary system which will enable it to negotiate on behalf of those who are aggrieved or who feel they are aggrieved under the terms of the resolution.
Mr. Speaker, I was of the opinion that we could not put the terms of this resolution into legislative form, but after discussing the problem with several competent persons I think a general principle could be written into the various acts to give this protection. One bill could be formulated which would include the terms of the resolution as they affect a large number of acts. I am concerned that we might spend weeks and weeks discussing all the acts that would be involved to which this principle would apply, such as the Official Languages Act, the Public Service Act, the Armed Forces Act-you name it. The principle applies to almost every act that involves civil servants. If the government really wishes to make this a firm declaration, then I suggest it should be a firm declaration and the only way that can be ensured, Mr. Speaker, is to have it in written form.
It has been suggested by my leader that this protection should be written into the collective agreements and this is certainly worth considering. He says it is better than writing it into the law. That may be so. We argued that the bill of rights was not of much value, that its provisions
Official Languages
should be written into the constitution. In fact, over the years the bill of rights has been used on a limited number of occasions with success in the courts because there has been an air of unreality in the way it has been applied by the courts. History might well prove that the same situation will apply in this case, and that legislation may be developed out of this resolution. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any member in this House who is not ashamed of his lack of ability to enforce the terms of this resolution as it applies to the civil service.
Members of this House who sat on the estimates committee actually considered the members of the parliamentary security staff one by one. They said, for instance, that such and such a man is French, and another is English; that such and such a man has a French name but does not speak French, and this one only speaks a little English. Mr. Speaker, we played the numbers game. We are not interested in equality of opportunity, but played the numbers game. The members wanted so many men to be on this side, and so many on that side. I am referring, of course, to the linguilistic capability of the men. There was nothing anybody on the committee could do about it, because that was the attitude of many members who support either side of this particular argument. The fact is that we started adding up numbers and the committee said, "We want so many in this group and so many in that group." There was no reference to whether or not we had introduced criteria on how to promote people who are competent, about whether we have given opportunities for people to learn a second language, if that is necessary, or how it would be possible to promote people in areas where a second language is not necessary. We did not do that at all. Instead, we played the numbers game. I think most members of that committee are ashamed that we played that game.
I think this resolution is only a pious resolution unless it really provides some protection for civil servants, and provides it without it being necessary for the civil servant to make a lot of fuss. We are well aware of the number of civil servants in Ottawa who have tried to make a case about their position. How has that benefited them, Mr. Speaker? In the long run it may benefit the country, because what they had to say was of value in the decision making process. But, Mr. Speaker, those proceedings did not do anything for the people involved. In every instance of which I know, the people concerned did not resign voluntarily; they were forced to leave the civil service, and nothing was done on their behalf by the associations. The associations did not protect them. So, I am not enamoured with the role the associations have played in the past. It may be that they will do better from now on. I suggest, however, that unless the government is really interested in providing the kind of protection of which I speak, the resolution before the House will turn out to be nothing more than a pious resolution. It will be nothing more than a pious exercise unless the government is willing to provide protection; otherwise, these principles will be changed, and changed very likely according to the fortunes of the political parties in this House.
At present, the members are being asked to endorse a program that was not introduced by a majority govern-

Official Languages
ment. It is a program that was introduced by a minority government led by Mr. Pearson. It introduced these proposals. They have already been applied in the government's operations, if one is to judge by a public release of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury). The civil service has had to abide by the terms of the program. That announcement has been made, but it was made two or three days after the election. That was not soon enough to save Mr. Blair or Mr. Francis. But, that announcement was made, and protection is being provided for the civil servants. Mr. Speaker, I do not want to see, after another election, another declaration made by the President of the Treasury Board, or whoever may be making the declaration, regarding a list of points that are to govern this issue. I should like to see the kind of protection of which I have spoken agreed to by most members of the House, in the same way as almost every member supported the official languages bill. On the other hand, if we leave this matter so that there is doubt, and leave it in such a way that the individual civil servant will not have the right to apply for the protection suggested in this resolution, it seems to me there will be a lot of monkeying around with these rules.
I agree with the Leader of the New Democratic Party who thinks there are going to be changes in this matter. I agree; I think there will be changes, but there will not be changes in the terms of this resolution. There are going to be changes in how the terms of this resolution will be applied in various departments. I am sure that there will be differences of opinion over whether a deputy minister, say, of a particular department, should be bilingual or not. However, I am sure, and I hope other members agree, that such matters can be negotiated by the associations of the civil service. However, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the government itself will indicate that this resolution is not the end of this matter, but that legislative action will be taken to implement the terms of the resolution.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a distinct privilege for me to be confused with the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) and the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan) on the same day, as both members are about 20 years my junior. I appreciate the honour you do me.
My hon. friend from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), for whom I have great affection, left me in some doubt at the conclusion of his speech as to whether he would support the amendment proposed by the leader of my party or not. I can only conclude from his last few remarks that he will not support it. I will. If the amendment does not carry, I will support the original resolution. I say that so that members of the House and the people of this country can know right now that, despite the published reports in what pass for newspapers in this city, the overwhelming majority of my colleagues in the Progressive Conservative party will also support it.
I think we have to make clear at the outset of every address by every member of the House that we are not debating here the merits of the Official Languages Act or the merits of the bilingual policy of Canada. Those are

matters of public policy and were decided upon four years ago. All the parties in this House supported that position, and it is now a fact. We are discussing here a resolution which, if its principles are honoured, will extend greater job security to as many as a quarter of a million Canadians. That is all we are discussing.

people who invoke the constitution. They invoke it on both sides. We have not been able to find a way to even repatriate our constitution. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told us here last week in what I thought was an excellent speech, it is not matter of history, but a matter of hard political reality. We have to cope with it here and we have to cope with it responsibly.
I want to address myself to an issue the Prime Minister has raised many times, both in this House and outside, national unity. We were told on many occasions that it was necessary to maintain the Liberal government in office because they and they alone were concerned with national unity. I have a different concept of national unity than wanting to make sure that the Official Languages Act is enshrined for all time. It is an important issue and I do not wish to denigrate it. However, alongside some of the other pressing issues that face this country, it is relatively minor and elitist because it concerns a small number of people.
The danger to national unity does not reside in whether this or that resolution passes this House. The danger to national unity lies in the fact that this government and governments before it for 100 years have not cared enough about the problems that vex the daily lives of the people in this country. In Montreal a few years ago, a handful of dispossessed and disaffected people rebelled. What did the government do? Did it prevail on the old friend of the Prime Minister, the mayor of Montreal, to build some houses? Did it prevail upon the city of Montreal to provide more green space and clean up the water and air? Did it give its attention to the children in the slums which have been described by the late Saul Alinsky as the worst in North America? The government did not do any of those things. It busied itself by trying to throw as many citizens in this country in jail as it could.
We do not need secret police groups operating in the East Block. That will not help national unity. What we need is a government that will know every time a child grows up in a slum the government is responsible. What we need is a government that will know that every time a woman is mangled or killed at the hands of some unskilled abortionist because no legal way is open to her the government is responsible. What we need is a government that will know every time an old person rots away in a tenement with an insufficient amount of money at the end of his or her life that the government is responsible. The government, in order to deserve to continue to be the government, must address itself to these problems because these are the real problems to national unity in Canada.

speechtext:
In any event, Mr. Speaker, the two-nation thesis has long been rejected.
This government has in the past been accused by some people as being overly preoccupied with the question of bilingualism, especially as it relates to the public service. Well, as long as there are instances when the public service does not whenever feasible and whenever there is

the need, as was documented in the two annual reports of the Commissioner of Official Languages, deal with the public in English and in French according to the public's choice; and as long as the public service does not, as I shall illustrate, offer equal opportunities to French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians to work in the language of their choice, I maintain that this alleged preoccupation is warranted. Indeed, there are good grounds for arguing that it should probably be intensified.
While I will be speaking this afternoon primarily on how this declaration affects Francophones, let us not for a moment forget that it is directed at both major linguistic groups in Canada; that it offers certain guarantees, and certain rights to both English-speaking and to Frenchspeaking public servants and to any Canadian who wishes to work for the public service.
Let us remember that the public service is the prime instrument through which federal laws and regulations are administered. It is the single largest employer in Canada. It is one of the sinews which binds together our geographically diverse country with its linguistically heterogeneous population. Thus, it is critically important that the public service reflect in its compositions the population of the country. Given the Canadian reality of 16 million English-speaking and 6 million French-speaking inhabitants, clearly it is essential for the sake of national unity and for the sake of rendering effective services to ensure that in all government departments there are sufficient materials and personnel to serve the public in English and in French according to its choice, and for English and French to enjoy equal status as languages of work within the public service so that everyone will feel at home.
Although this is neither the time nor the place to examine in detail the history of bilingualism in the public service, it is nevertheless appropriate to note that for many years, indeed for generations, Francophone Canadians have voiced their concern for the need to have a public service which could deal with them in French, and in which they could work in French. However, it is only since the early 1960's that governments at the federal level have taken a serious interest in attempting to realize these goals.
If it seems to some people that there is too much government activity on the question of bilingualism, this may appear to be the case to them because so little was done concerning this vital issue prior to the mid 1960's.
This past decade has witnessed a desire for epanouisse-ment among many groups in Canadian society-certain injustices against minorities were certainly not willingly committed. We have a certain amount of catching up to do as regards minority rights and so it is that today we speak of the rights of women, the rights of natives and of ethnic groups. The French-speaking minority is now living through that catching up period. Francophone minorities look upon Canadian federalism as an economic union and also as an association, a socio-cultural and linguistic agreement which strives towards the same goal-a prosperous Canada, endowed with two official languages and several cultures.
The premise of my argument will be to establish that the existence of francophone minorities in Canada guaran-
June 5, 1973

tees the objective of the government's resolution, that is a functional, bilingual federal institution. If we are to avoid, Quebec becoming the only place where francophones can feel that they are able to live and work in French and becoming the homeland for all francophone Canadians, it is essential that the federal government take effective measures to implement institutional bilingualism and provide increased opportunity for francophones who desire to do so to work in French.
The motion that we are discussing today constitutes one of this government's attempts to realize these goals. Unless francophones can identify, to the extent that anglophones do, the federal public service as being their public service and the national capital as being their capital, the continued existence of a strongly united Canada from sea to sea is threatened. For a federation can exist only as long as its constituent parts feel that they are a vital part of the federation. History is replete with examples which substantiate this point.
That federal bilingual institution will be functional inasmuch as the supply of institutional bilingualism meets a firm demand throughout the country. However, in provinces where anglophones a're in majority, the guarantee of that demand rests on francophone and bilingual minorities which have that responsibility and even that obligation.
In 1973 in Canada, there are 926,105 francophones living in provinces where anglophones are in majority. Those bilingual Canadians whose mother tongue is French fought for their rights since Confederation. Indeed they fought for their education rights to be recognized by the province. School being the extension of the family, it was a guarantee for the survival and development of their own entity. However, it is true that the French minorities outside Quebec have had to organize, to protect their rights, their mother tongue. They did so at their own expenses, at the cost of great sacrifices.
Mr. Speaker, I talked about that problem in this House last March 20, and I quote from page 2431 of Hansard where I said:
All efforts made by the federal government will be of little use if we cannot maintain in all provinces a strong, lively, and dynamic French-speaking group which would lead the way and make a place for itself under the sun thanks to all sorts of provincial and public institutions designed to promote and encourage the French culture.
I continued later:
Those efforts towards the establishment of bilingualism, Francophones have made them since our country was founded, but under present circumstances, the francophone minority can no longer oppose single-handed the anglophone giant of unilingual-ism. They must be given specific and efficient help if they are to continue living and fulfilling themselves in French.
The great majority of unilingual English-speaking people enjoyed a good education system which was tailored to their economic resources. For some of them in public service who make an application for a management job or who hold a position which eventually will be designated bilingual, they have merely to perfect their qualifications by becoming bilingual.
Official Languages
The principle of equal opportunities in public service is very important for us. Unhappily, because of a defective education system in their own language, the great majority of French-speaking minorities have no access to the middle or higher echelons of management. In 1965, in Ontario, where 500,000 French-speaking Canadians are now living, a very low percentage of bilingual Frenchspeaking Canadians were continuing their secondary education beyond grade 10. The large majority were bilingual owing to the force of circumstances and the importance to express themselves in both languages. On the other hand, they were disadvantaged with respect to formal, academic, technical and vocational education because there were no French public schools.
Fortunately this situation has changed in recent years. Even if the battle will always be difficult, at least in Ontario-you just have to read the daily papers to realize it-the present school generation will eventually have opportunities of access to the public service with the same academic, technical and vocational ability as the English unilingual applicant.
The principle in the second part of the resolution under study has almost not been applied as regards bilingual French Canadians now in the public service. They did not have that adequate technical, vocational and administrative training that their English fellow-citizens had.
Joining the public service and staying there at a lower level cannot be considered as equal opportunity. To have equal opportunity means being able, depending on one's abilities and one's own merits, to reach the middle and top management levels. It is surprising and even ironic to note that the federal government in the fall of 1972 had sponsored 21,000 civil servants, especially among the intermediate and higher ranks, 80 per cent of whom are English-speaking, who had registered for French courses. The unilingual English Canadian was thus provided with the double qualification of bilingualism.
Do the sincere English-speaking groups, whose socioeconomic classes had enabled them to acquire a higher education in their own language, appreciate that bilingual measure of the government and consider for a moment the unfairness done to French-speaking minorities too often disillusioned and frustrated?
Have such groups of right-minded and honest Canadians thought that to benefit really from equal opportunities the bilingual French-speaking Canadian would perhaps need a similar federal fund not to learn English but to enable them to better their own professional proficiency in the administrative and technical fields?
French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians do not enjoy equal opportunities to work in the public service in the language of their choice. It is the intention of the declaration to ensure that both English-speaking and French-speaking Canadians enjoy equal opportunity, when competing on the merit principle, to be appointed to the public service. Too often in discussions regarding this question the facts are neglected. I would now like to discuss some realities concerning this matter.
The 1971 annual report of the Public Service Commission states the language requirements of the 66,675 appointments made to the public Service during the year
26314-68 i

June 5, 1973

1971. The figures include both appointments of former public servants and the appointments of new employees. The language requirements of these are as follows: 5,509 or 8.3 per cent required French-language capacity only, 6,047 or 9.1 per cent bilingual capacity and 52,821 or 79.2 per cent required English capacity only; the language requirements for 2,298 positions, 3.4 per cent, were not indicated.
In his appearance before the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee the Commissioner of Official Languages presented data regarding the language requirements for the appointments made to the public service in the year 197273. The figures indicate that 7.6 per cent of the positions required bilingual capacity, 11 per cent required French only and 75.6 per cent required English only.
Furthermore it is quite widely known the underrepresentation of francophones in the public service is more pronounced in the upper than in the lower level positions, and that the opportunity to work in French decreases as one moves up the hierarchy of occupational levels. Granted, this declaration is not a panacea to all problems involving bilingualism in the public service. However, panacea's just don't exist for complex problems of this nature.
That is why it is a resolution, not a statute. It spells out in specific terms the guidelines being used for implementing bilingualism in the public service and for identifying bilingual positions. Let us remember that not all positions but approximately one tenth or 25,000 are slated to become bilingual positions.
After carefully examining the content of the resolution, I feel that no one can in all honesty claim that it contains any elements of injustice. The formal commitment by the federal government toward institutional bilingualism in the public service is relatively recent; it dates from April 6, 1966, the day the right hon. Mr. Pearson presented the declaration to the House of Commons.
One of the principles stated in that historic declaration was, and I quote:
-the linguistic and cultural values of both English speaking and French speaking Canadians will be reflected through civil service recruitment and training.
This national representation, well balanced and satisfactory, will include in our public service 10 per cent of bilingual employees and ensure as well that all unilingual Canadians have the right to work in the public service in the language of their choice.
Major changes in complex organizations, such as the federal public service, are rarely achieved without some friction. Institutional bilingualism, if it is to be effectively realized, will likely require both changes of an organizational nature and some changes in values within sectors of Canadian society. As politicians, as the elected representatives we can reduce the amount of friction involved by examining objectively the actual content of the government's policy regarding bilingualism in the public service. I think that it is due time to invest in the "bilingualiza-tion" of our unilingual citizens and that it is also essential to invest in the improvement of those who are bilingual. If we use all available assets to that effect, we will succeed in reaching our objective, that is respect for and development of our two great languages and cultures as well as the citizens concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, successive Canadian governments have been labouring for a decade to make it evident that the federal administration reflects the equal partnership of the French and English founding people. The constitution formally recognized both French and English in 1867 in the federal field and in the province of Quebec. However, it has become evident to us that this recognition was incomplete in many respects, and often disputed where the French language was concerned. The equal status of the two languages must be established without a shade of doubt. From now on, I will proceed in my mother tongue.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) waited a long time before introducing in this House his resolution on bilingualism. When he finally introduced it on April 13 last, Canadians were expecting a realistic proposal that could snatch the government policy on bilingualism out of the stand-pattism that has characterized it since the passing of the Official Languages Act. On April 13 last, Canadians were disappointed. Of course, it was not the first time that this government disappointed them, far from it.
But after publication of the Spicer report, which pointed out the numerous inadequacies of the bilingualism program as administered by this government, the government was expected at least to go in the direction shown by the Commissioner of Official Languages and take steps to give a new start to faltering programs on bilingualism in the public service.
Not only are the April 13 proposals not heralding a new start of the faltering programs on bilingualism, but they clearly show this government's intention to confine itself to fine statements and good intentions.
Things have improved very much since 1962 in the federal public service, in federal institutions, as far as bilingualism is concerned, and the struggles led in this House by the Creditist members for the recognition of the French fact are historical.
It is true. There was much progress and improvements to enable a French-speaking member or a French-speaking Canadian to feel at home everywhere in Canada.
But since 1969, not only was there no improvement, but conditions deteriorated unceasingly. The Liberal government passed the Official Languages Act and then thought that the bilingualism problem had been solved. As if pronouncements of goodwill were enough to make French exist in the federal administration.
Some people said that the government was trying to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds by passing a law on bilingualism without taking any positive action. As a matter of fact, what the government is doing is much worse than that: it is trying to get the hare to run after the hounds! It takes advantage of the good faith and confidence of English- and French-speaking Canadians.
The Social Credit party intends to bring an amendment aimed at giving a concrete bearing to the meaningless proposal made by the government on April 13 last. The
June 5, 1973

Social Credit party proposes specific measures which, if they are implemented, will bring an end to the everlasting debate on the language question and finally allow the House to tackle the economic problems of the country.
It is the failure of the government to take realistic measures on bilingualism which gave rise to the uneasiness existing in the civil service and within the population on this matter. What the Social Credit party is proposing is simple, but someone had to think of it. Instead of spending millions of dollars to try and teach a second language to civil servants who are a few years away from retirement, and instead of favouring injustice by trying to implement a quota system which goes against the principles of merit promotion, the government should consider creating two parallel administrations, one English and one French. Why should we force a second language on those who do not want it? Why should we spend millions of dollars for language courses which are bound to fail miserably?
The parallel administrations proposed by the Social Credit party represent the final and ultimate solution to the bilingualism problem in the civil service.
Let the government create, according to geographic and population circumstances, a French section and an English section in all departments, according to their respective administrative needs. Then, we will all be served and administered in the official language of our choice.
The employees of the civil service will be promoted exclusively on the basis of their respective merits without fearing racial and unjust policies.
This is in short what we propose: the adoption of logical and realistic measures to solve the problem of bilingualism in the civil service. The government therefore must stop beating about the bush and decide on a course of action. Everybody is sick and tired of listening to the commonplace remarks from the government side. While English-speaking Canadians feel they are being victimized, French-speaking Canadians want a federal administration in which they can feel at home.
The government must therefore make up their mind and assume their responsibilities; they must abandon these declarations of principles which are as empty as useless, and cope with the task of establishing parallel administrations in order to satisfy the true needs of the Canadian people.
This is what we are asking for in the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte); we request the support of all hon. members of good will so that this program which is in line with what all Canadians have been hoping for may be set in action.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this resolution as one who voted against the language bill in 1969. I should like to say that time has in no way changed my mind that the language bill has been and will continue to be a divisive factor in this country. Perhaps eventually the country will be divided, and it may well be that history will record the language bill as the final divisive force. I think any student of history would say that the relationship between the French province of Quebec and the balance of the country, mainly English-
Official Languages
speaking, has made for a very difficult, unstable nation, but this country has given its people freedom, a reasonable standard of living, and in the final analysis those are the most important things for any individual.
One of the differences between this debate and the one that took place in 1969 is the indication that the Rallie-ment des Creditistes members, speaking for their voters in the province of Quebec, have indicated that bilingualism does not answer the objectives of those members who gained 30 per cent of the popular vote in Quebec. These views cannot be disregarded. These hon. members have indicated by this amendment that the present bilingual program will not solve our language difficulties in the civil service. There is much to be commended in respect of this amendment, but with the creation of French-language units we are already moving in the direction of a dual or parallel civil administration as suggested. I welcome that viewpoint and agree with it. It is timely at this stage in that it gets the bilingual problem out of the area of being untouchable and the suggestion that if it is not embraced in its entirety, Canada will fall to pieces. This debate is now placed in the political area where a decision can be made on the basis of what can be accomplished.
The stand taken by hon. members of the Creditiste party would indicate that a sizeable number of Francophones do not see in the bilingual concept a rational and reasonable approach to the idea of a bilingual civil service. Time at this stage will not allow a considered comment on this amendment, but I have long been of the opinion, in a general way, that the thrust proposed by hon. members of that party is reasonable, right, and will get around many of the difficulties in which we now find ourselves.
The attitude of the Liberal government that all those who oppose the bilingual program are to be found only amongst the Anglophone population of the country, and that all those people are bigots, must now be discarded, because in the Francophone segment of our country there are substantial numbers who are not happy and presumably must be classified also as bigots. The hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) has stated in no uncertain terms that the present provision for bilingualism in the civil service will not in any way solve our problems. The sizeable number of voters in the province of Quebec who place their trust in the Social Credit party would indicate there is a large group of Quebecers who are looking for other means of satisfying their aspirations than the Official Languages Act, and I doubt that the Social Credit party at the last election numbered many Westmount Rhodesians among their supporters.
The attempt by the language bill to create a bilingual civil service to solve the French-English problem has created more difficulties than it has helped. Few would question the right of Canadians to receive federal government service in their official language, but it is an entirely different thing to make the civil service bilingual and to make all public servants speak both languages. This is an intellectual solution to a very difficult problem. It is a solution that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), being bilingual, has arrived at by the following process of reasoning: "We have a French-English problem ... I am bilingual . . . others are bilingual; we will solve this problem by making everybody bilingual".

June 5, 1973
Official Languages
Having two official languages creates very great problems. This has been the case in all countries where there are a number of languages spoken. We only have to consider Belgium and South Africa to appreciate the great problems involved. The fundamental difficulty lies in the fact that no individual is bilingual. Everyone has a mother tongue and a working knowledge of a second language. Most people can say a few words in another language, but to be able to converse and work in the second language requires a high degree of proficiency in the language.
The measure of the bilingual ability of a person is of necessity an extremely subjective judgment and open to wide interpretation. For instance, a person may be grammatically correct in his use of the second language but his accent may make it impossible for anyone to understand him. I am sure that all members of the House would prefer that a witness in a committee who is making a valiant attempt to speak a second language, and often being grammatically correct, would speak in his first language and allow the interpreters to translate his remarks.
Functional bilingualism has always been present and would have served our needs adequately had we followed a sensible language policy. The present Official Languages Act allows for recruitment of civil servants on the basis of their linguistic abilities without regard for the merit of the candidates concerned. In view of the present structure of our civil service, we will shortly have a civil service whose prime aim will be language competence. It will be composed of an elite whose goal of excellence will be language training and who will be unaware of the fact that their primary function is to serve the public.
No one would deny that the civil service, as set up before the Official Languages Act, created a hardship for unilingual francophones. Remedial measures could have been introduced, and in fact were introduced in many cases and acted upon, to increase the percentage of francophones up to their census representation. Before the Official Languages Act was brought in it was difficult for unilingual francophones to enter the civil service, but anglophones from all over the country had an opportunity to obtain employment in the civil service in Ottawa. The principles of bilingualism slam the door shut to all unilingual Canadians, both francophones and anglophones, and make it impossible for them to participate in the federal civil service. If the civil service was previously biased against the French speaking minority, the present act is biased against unilingual Canadians, both francophones and anglophones. The present civil service is recruited from a small group of people in Canada who are bilingual by circumstance, and therefore it is not representative of the country at large.
The fact that Canada is made up of 16 million anglophones who speak little French and 6 million francophones, the majority of whom speak no English, means that that segment of the population which is bilingual is francophone by circumstance. It has been widely suggested that only 10 per cent of the civil servants will be required to be bilingual, but when one considers that this 10 per cent will be made up of civil servants in the top executive echelons-the people who make the decisions and carry on the daily business of the government-one
(Mr. Ritchie.]
realizes that an almost impossible situation will arise. Those people will have to be recruited from the small group of Canadians who are bilingual, and experience proves that these are francophones.
It is entirely unthinkable and unacceptable that this top 10 per cent of civil servants who are francophones should dominate the vast majority of civil servants who happen to be anglophones. Only if the top level of the civil service were to represent the numerical language ration of the country at large would the present bilingualism policy be acceptable. It is bad enough for the majority to dominate the minority, but for a minority to dominate the majority is intolerable.
We may well wonder why this resolution was not incorporated into the Language Act, because now it has no legal validity. The reason is that the people of Canada in the election of 1972 indicated their very grave concern about the language policy of this government. Language difficulties and unrest are increasing. Indeed, it is one of the major issues in the Air Canada strike. This unrest will certainly increase as time passes.
A much more practical solution to our language problem is available. So far as language is concerned, our country is divided, with Quebec being the main centre of the francophone population and most of the rest of the country being mainly anglophone. Western Canada especially is now becoming unilingual anglophone. The development of a dual civil service is an easy and practical way of bringing harmony to the language groups in Canada. There is no reason why a unilingual francophone should have to learn a second language to advance in the civil service, or vice-versa. The civil service could be structured in such a way as to recognize the basic principles of providing service in both languages. For those' who say that a dual civil service would be too expensive, let me point out that we must recognize the enormous expense of providing language training in our attempt to make our civil service bilingual.
The resolution brought forward by the government makes no sense and carries no weight with anyone. At best, it can be said to be a moral directive to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) so long as the present incumbent occupies this position. It is not binding on any of the selection committees of the civil service. The only logical reason for bringing forth the resolution, which is intended to reaffirm legislation already passed, is a political one. It is an attempt by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to ensure his political base in Quebec and to continue to humiliate anglophones in the rest of Canada. It is an attempt on his part to show his superiority as a bilingual person over unilingual Canadians. It certainly attempts to demonstrate that all unilingual Canadians are second class citizens in this country.
The indication which the government gave that it will not accept amendments from the opposition to put the resolution into law demonstrates that the government does not intend to abide by the resolution. If the principles of the resolution are not put into legislation, even lip service will not be given to the aims it attempts to achieve. Regardless of whether the guidelines in the resolution are incorporated in the act, they will not be very effective. Even the clause which makes it possible for a unilingual
June 5, 1973

person to apply for a position that is designated as bilingual means very little in fact because, practically speaking, the job will always have to be given to a bilingual person. A department head will be reluctant to allow a position to remain vacant for a year while the new employee is learning a second language.
To give an example of this let me quote an official who spoke in the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration on the staffing process. He had the following to say:
Mr. Chairman, we have developed a process, a staffing process within the department, whereby positions that are considered to require bilingualism to fulfill the duties are open to all employees of the department. In the event that a unilingual person is considered to be the best person in a competition and that a properly qualified bilingual person does not qualify, under those circumstances, the unilingual person is awarded the appointment-
Does this not indicate that only in exceptional cases, where no suitable bilingual person is available, does a unilingual person have any chance of getting a job? In a practical way, one cannot quarrel with any department head who would want the position filled at the earliest opportunity.
The Official Languages Act has created a great deal of disunity and divisiveness. In this resolution we are concerned about the effect of the act on people already in the civil service. But I have always said that if we are to make everybody in the civil service bilingual, we could put everyone who is unilingual on pension and we would even then be farther ahead. It is slowly and surely coming home to unilingual Canadians that the civil service in Ottawa is closed to them. There is a realization in unilingual western Canada that there will be little chance for people from that area in the Ottawa scene. There are those who say that there should be a greater degree of second language teaching in schools across the country, but it is certain that in western Canada there is little point in learning French as the second language. In my area, for every person who goes to Quebec, 20 go to Mexico, so if there is any stimulus for learning a second language, the preference would be for Spanish. Internationally, French is used relatively little compared to Russian, German, and, I suppose eventually, the Oriental languages.
We can forecast that in western Canada there will be a steady decline in the teaching and use of French as the second language. This might be regrettable, but I do not think this trend can be reversed, and indeed it would make little sense to attempt to reverse it. The Official Languages Act makes the western Canadian feel more strange, more apart from Ottawa. Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I support the amendment put forward by my party. I think it will improve the resolution and put some teeth in it. Otherwise, the resolution, as it now stands, is not worth the ink with which it was written.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Marchand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to take part in the debate on this important resolution. The importance of our debate on this fundamental question of bilingualism in the public service cannot be overstated. There is nothing more and nothing less at stake than this country of ours, Canada. I am very
Official Languages
pleased with the support that the various groups representing the public service have pledged to the principles embodied in this resolution. I cannot help but believe, too, that the well-being and good will of our political system in Canada will also be strengthened by the affirmation of this resolution.
I have followed the debate closely and with great interest, and would like to pay tribute to the hon. members who have spoken strongly in favour of the resolution, particularly the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), the leader of the NDP, and many others. I know that questions were raised on the other side of the House by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) and the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly) on why we introduced this resolution. One of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain was that we were trying to divide his party, among other things. Mr. Speaker, this could not be farther from the truth.
I would like to say very sincerely that I have admired the way in which the Leader of the Official Opposition has conducted himself on this question. He has been unwavering in his stand. He has not varied one iota in the stand he has taken on the question of bilingualism, and I commend him for that.
In gathering together a few ideas for my remarks today, several thoughts crossed my mind. The first is that it is a well known fact that I am neither of French nor English ancestry, and therefore I have no particular axe to grind. I might also say I have some real questions about the theory of the two founding races as expressed by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard), because my ancestors knew this land well before either of those groups arrived.
A second thought, and one that greatly disturbed me, was particularly relevant during the last election campaign and its immediate aftermath. We did not talk much about national unity, bilingualism, and the other ties that bind our diverse country together. We assumed, rather naively, that a great deal of the stress which had fostered disunity and misunderstanding in Canada had been alleviated over the years. We, as a government and as a parliament, failed to demonstrate the true spirit and the real facts behind bilingualism.
In my own campaign I talked about national unity as often as I could. At all-candidates-forums, coffee parties, townhall meetings and so on I, like the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), encountered very few red necks whom one could call bigots for their stand on bilingualism. However, I did encounter a lot of misunderstanding about the application of bilingualism in the public service.
The last parliament gave nearly unanimous support to the Official Languages Act in 1969. However, in my view, as parliamentarians we failed to demonstrate the leadership that was necessary to explain the rationale of the act, as it was being implemented, to the people of Canada. We cannot permit a situation where misunderstandings like that can develop, with the racial tensions that such misunderstandings might heighten in the future.
Several other thoughts hit me. In addition to being of neither French nor English ancestry, I am a western Canadian and a former civil servant. From the way some

June 5, 1973
Official Languages
people have been ranting over the years one would assume that I have all the credentials to be one of the most anti-bilingualism people in the country. This is not so. I believe that the great majority of Canadians would support this resolution. But it is seldom that this group grab the headlines because, quite frankly and sadly, the positive beliefs that they hold just do not rate headlines.
No one can or will deny that there are certain forces in Canada which seek to subvert the unity of the nation. The Official Languages Act and its application are a target of this narrow, vindictive group. But Canadians are a tolerant people, and I am confident that they will continue to pay little attention to the small minority whose narrow outlook on life permits them to play to the basest of human emotions, fear, hatred and bigotry, emotions which result largely from a sad lack of knowledge and understanding.
From my point of view, a very important consideration with respect to this entire question centres squarely on my own ancestry. I feel very strongly that there is no way that Canada, as a nation, can recognize the rich heritage and diversity of the many groups that have joined together to build the great nation of Canada, and that will continue to work together in the future, if we do not give vital recognition to the principles and the application of bilingualism and multiculturalism. The eventual result of adopting a narrow approach would be for Canada to become a melting pot, like our neighbour to the south. This is directly contrary to the spirit and the vigour of Canada-a spirit of unity amidst diversity.
I believe that our government has committed itself to the right course for the cultural survival of Canada. I believe that our multiculturalism program, and its vigorous application, will help remove a lot of the misunderstanding which exists among several segments in Canada with respect to the bilingualism program. Multiculturalism and bilingualism and biculturalism go hand in hand in the recognition of human rights in this land of ours. These elements cannot be separated, nor can the spirit which underlies them.
We have heard several people say, particularly in western Canada, that the government is shoving French down our throats. They also complain about the cost of the bilingualism programs. Those two statements are probably the most common manifestation of the lack of knowledge of this program which exists in certain parts of the nation. It is our duty to do a better job of telling it the way it is. No one is forcing anyone to do or learn anything because of the act or this resolution, and I firmly believe that the cost of the program is small when one stops and considers what is at stake-Canada. Mr. Speaker, we may not all be able to speak to each other in either of the official languages but all of us, as Canadians, must be able to speak to each other with our hearts. When it comes to understanding what this whole issue is all about, it is heartfelt understanding that is all important.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate briefly for the purpose of saying a few words with respect to what I believe is the one and only issue before the House of Commons. Certain-

ly, the issue that I wish to pinpoint in a moment is the only one that is now dividing us in this debate.
We do not have before us the question of the Official Languages Act or the question of bilingualism in Canada; we do not have before us an amendment relating to bilingual districts or to the activities of the Commissioner of Official Languages. All we have before us is a resolution that relates to employees in the Public Service of Canada in so far as the language question affects them.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that even the resolution which is before us in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and which contains nine main principles, is not now an issue. I realize that when the vote comes there may be some who will vote against it but it is clear that the vote for the resolution, whether it is amended or not, will be overwhelming. I realize that there are those who have argued that it was not necessary to bring this resolution before the House of Commons, but in any case now that it is here it does not divide us; we are agreed that the principles set out in the Prime Minister's resolution ought to be applied with regard to employment in the public service. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, that leaves us in this position; that the only issue-and it is the only one I am going to talk about-is whether those principles should simply be endorsed by a vote of the House of Commons in favour of the Prime Minister's motion or whether those principles should be written into the law, namely, into the Official Languages Act, the Public Service Employment Act, the Public Service Staff Relations Act and several others referred to as "appropriate statutes".
Sir, I do not fault the Leader of the Opposition or the seconder of this motion, who is my good friend and neighbour, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), for submitting their amendment and for making the case for it in terms of their wanting to get as much of a guarantee as is possible for the public servants in whom they are interested. If I may put it in the simplest terms, it just happens that I do not agree with them. I, too, happen to be concerned about the rights of public servants. As most if not all members are aware, I am concerned for them when they reach the point of retirement but I am also concerned about their rights as working public servants.
I am terribly aware, as is the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton who stated his position yesterday and as is the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly) who spoke today, of the agony and fear that were experienced by many public servants in the national capital region and other parts of Canada when the guidelines being applied by the Treasury Board and the government in general were less favourable to the rights of public servants than would be the case if these guidelines came into effect. Therefore, I readily understand their desire to see these better guidelines given as much force, as much guarantee as is possible.
Even so, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the matter of the language question as it applies to employment in the public service is one that is still being sorted out. It is my information, not only from what I have read in the newspapers but from my talks with officials in the public

service unions, that they are tremendously satisfied with the measure of consultation that they had with the government in the drawing up of these guidelines. That satisfaction is not retroactive-it does not go back to some earlier circumstances but I understand that so far as the consultations that resulted in the drawing up of these guidelines were concerned, they were fully satisfactory. But the officials of those same public service unions I believe-and I say this to my good friends from Grenville-Carleton and Ottawa West-I believe that they speak for their members, I believe that they speak for the public servants of Canada generally and particularly for the public servants in the Ottawa area when they say that they do not want even these guidelines to be frozen into our statutes, to be given the rigidity of law. To use their own language, they say there are still some "bugs" to be worked out, there are still some points to be made clear. When one looks at the resolution one sees in it, for example, a couple of dates which may well have to be moved forward or backward and there are other points which, in the course of two or three years might well need to be changed.
I believe that the leaders of the Public Service Alliance of Canada and the Professional Institute of the Public Service Canada are quite right in their contention that they want the present situation to obtain, they want still to be able to engage in consultation with the Treasury Board and with the government to work out the best possible arrangements in this area. It may come, the other side of 1978, that it might be a good idea to put principles in this area into our law. I am not even sure of that. I am not one of those who say this would be all right for a few years from now but it just is not all right now; I am not even sure it would be right a few years from now.
Along with my tremendous respect for the force of law and living by the rule of law, I also have great respect for the principle of consultation and collective bargaining. Precisely because this whole matter is the sensitive one that it is, precisely because it is such a human situation calling for consultation, I call on my friends who have placed this amendment before the House not to press it to a vote. I am not expecting to persuade them to withdraw it, but I plead with them not to press it to a vote. I plead with them to listen to my argument and my appeal. I am trying to do this not in terms of a confrontation. Rather, I believe that the spokesmen for the public servants of Canada are right in their contention that the best way to work this out, to continue the process of arriving at an agreement, is to leave it on the basis of consultation and not to write it into the law with all of the rigidity that can result therefrom.
I am doing my best to refer to my Ottawa friends in the affectionate terms that we sometimes use in the House of Commons. I have already done so with respect to the two at the west end of the city, and I hope the hon. member for Ottawa West will not mind if I say that I smiled a bit this afternoon when he said that laws are not inflexible-we change them all the time. In fact, his words were "It happens every day of the week". Now, my good friend from Ottawa West knows better and if he does not I ask him to consult the public servants of Ottawa. They know, for example, that there are improvements they would like in the Public Service Employment Act and in the Public
Official Languages
Service Staff Relations Act. Do we get amendments to those pieces of legislation every day of the week? We have not had an amendment to either of them since they were passed in 1967 or 1968. I remind him also of a piece of legislation of which all public servants in those constituencies and throughout Canada are aware, namely, the Public Service Superannuation Act. We scored a great victory here in 1969 and 1970 when we obtained the provision for the escalation of the pensions of retired public servants. However, there was written into the law on that occasion a provision that limits that escalation to 2 per cent per year, no matter how much the cost of living might rise in any one year. There have been recommendations galore, in fact, there are recommendations from advisory committees in this field, to the effect that that 2 per cent ceiling be removed.

speechtext: I see my hon. friend for Grenville-Carleton and my hon. friend for Ottawa West applauding. And if there are any other members from the Ottawa area here, they will applaud, too. No, Mr. Speaker, this goes on and on and on-

speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker; although I have great affection for the hon. member, I do not believe he has interpreted correctly what I said. I said that it was precisely because laws are not flexible that it is desirable, when enshrining the working rights of a quarter of a million Canadians, to do it in such a way as to remove the possibility of day to day amendment. I did say also that if a law was found, after a reasonable period, to be unworkable, it could be amended, and we do that here all the time. That is the business in which we are engaged. I did not mean to suggest that laws are flexible. They are certainly not, and it is the opposite meaning that I seek.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not quarrel with the hon. member's restatement of what he said earlier. I thought it was a correct restatement. There were two aspects to that comment, as he has now confirmed, namely, that one of the benefits of law is that it is inflexible, that it is there as a guarantee. But he also said the other thing, and it is the other thing on which I wish to comment. He suggested that when a law needs to be changed, it can be done easily. It happens every day of the week.

speechtext:
I have sat in this House when parties of both political stripes have been in control of the government and I remember how long it

June 5, 1973
Official Languages
took, with Liberals or Tories in power, to make headway in the area of superannuation to which I just referred. It is unfortunate right now that the 2 per cent ceiling in the Superannuation Act is there and, although there are recommendations galore for change, and although I think everybody is for that change, we have not been able to get that change, because the government is not willing to bring in the necessary bill.
I realize that we must have law, and we must have a firm law. We must know what it says. Yet, surely, in dealing with an area that is as sensitive as this, an area concerning the day to day lives of a quarter of a million Canadians, we should not put these principles into the form of a rigid law at least until we have got the bugs worked out, at least until those who are involved in the operation are satisfied that we have principles that can be put into law without doing damage to any of those 250,000 or 275,000 Canadians who work in the public service.
Speaking of law, Mr. Speaker, and I took a look at the act, in order to be sure of what I am saying, the Official Languages Act as it stands says almost nothing on this issue. There are no details in the Official Languages Act about employment in the public service. Indeed, the only reference to the subject is found in the very last subsection of the Official Languages Act where it is said that the public service must carry out the principles and aims of the Official Languages Act, subject always to the maintenance of the principles of selection of personnel according to merit as required by the Public Service Employment Act. There is some argument about that. Actually, a great deal of the trouble last year was over whether or not the merit principle had been set aside. I draw hon. member's attention to the suggestion that this be solved in the manner suggested in one of the paragraphs of the Prime Minister's resolution which reads:
that a knowledge of English and French is one of the elements of merit in the selection of candidates for bilingual positions;
I think it is a good idea that there be such a resolution, and I think it ought to be looked at, studied and worked on; but, until it has been tried and until it has been found that it is a proper way to interpret the merit principle, I do not think it would be a good idea to write it into the statute. So, one might go to the various other things that are in the resolution and one might comment on the Official Languages Act and the other statutes that apply in this field, such as the Public Service Employment Act and the Public Service Staff Relations Act.
We are dealing with a terribly important, terribly sensitive and real human situation, and I am glad that there are persons like the officials who speak for public servants through the staff associations and who are concerned about this. I think we should leave the matter in their hands, to be resolved by consultation between them and the Treasury Board. They are alert. If they are being exploited or led down the garden path or let down, we will hear from them. Moreover, we are here, ourselves, to hear directly from public servants if these rules are not being applied.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we would be buying more trouble, not less, if at this stage of the game we were to put these principles into law. They are good. Again, I do not fault my friends of the Progressive Conservative party for

having gone all the way, for having accepted them and for having said that they are so good we should make them law. I suggest, however, that we are still dealing with a human situation and that the best way to take care of it is through the process of consultation. My belief that the consultation has been satisfactory is not based merely on what the Prime Minister or the President of the Treasury Board said; it is based upon what representatives of the public service unions themselves have said. They like the present setup. I think it should continue. I believe that when we pass this resolution in the form in which it is before us in the name of the Prime Minister, it will not be simply a case of our approving these nine points; it will be a case of our giving our moral support and endorsation to what the public servants themselves are doing to resolve this important issue. On that basis we are prepared to support the motion as it was introduced.
