subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say at the outset that I support the contents of the resolution before us. More important, I support the amendment put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). I am proud to associate myself with his very thoughtful and responsible remarks in this debate. Let me assure him that his scars will soon heal. As a close observer of the last parliament, I remember vividly the debate in 1969 on the Official Languages Act. It was an important debate. With the enactment of that act, an important milestone in Canada's history was achieved. Members of the 28th parliament can be justly proud of their work at that time.
One of the great surprises to me as a new member of this House has been to observe since January of this year the process by which this government determines the order and substance of the business of the House. One would think that legislation urgently required by the nation would have first priority. Certainly, such legislation might

well bear some relationship to the promises and programs put forward in the previous election campaign and as a result of that campaign. Clearly, the economic issues were the principal issues discussed during the election campaign, at least in my part of the country, and one could hardly have faulted the government for introducing a series of economic measures following on the heels of that campaign.
Also, one would think that the order and substance of the business of the House might be determined by various events that suddenly occur, requiring immediate governmental action. The House, much to its credit, functioned along these lines last January with a resolution respecting the resumption of bombing in Viet Nam. In my view, this was a proper matter to be considered at that time. I was glad that Canada was able to speak forcefully and with one voice through the resolution put forward and adopted at that time.
But what have we here? Does the resolution before us represent a positive measure promised during an election campaign or a measure urgently required because of emergency circumstances? No. It involves essentially a matter dealt with in principle by the last parliament. It involves measures accepted by all parties in the House in the last parliament and enacted into law. I thought the principles of the Official Languages Act of 1969 were good. The principle of providing federal government services to Canadians in the official language of their choice is and was important. Also, the principle of providing access to the federal courts and all criminal courts in either official language was an important step forward. The office of Commissioner of Official Languages was created to be a sort of linguistic ombudsman. This has been, and will continue to be a most important and necessary function.
Why then do we need this resolution before us? It is not an amendment to the Public Service Employment Act or the Official Languages Act. It will have no force of law. It will not be binding on those administering the law. Perhaps we in this House can agree that there have been problems in administering the legislation. Even the government benches have conceded as much. Since 1969, it has been found that unilingual civil servants, both English and French, require special protection in the process of implementing this legislation. The nine points could provide this much needed protection if the government had chosen to give them the force of law. But it did not. It could have introduced the nine points as regulations under the act and thus given them legal effect, subject to scrutiny by the Statutory Instruments Committee. But it did not.
Instead, the government introduced a resolution designed to force all members of parliament to-to use the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) own words of January 8- "stand up and be counted". Yet the very form in which the matter was introduced negates any legal responsibility on the part of the government to see that the principles are adhered to, even if the resolution were unanimously adopted. It is playing politics with bilingualism in a way which can only be described as cowardly. At a time when diplomatic leadership is needed to assure Canadians, both French and English, that we can live together as a nation

under a strong government in Ottawa, we have a Machiavellian resolution politically designed to open old wounds and cause them to fester once again. What kind of contribution to national unity is this? Is it the only game the Prime Minister really knows how to play?
Obviously, there are two courses one can follow in response to a contrived scheme such as this. One is to vote against the resolution. I cannot do this because the principles and protection enunciated are too important to run the risk of my being misunderstood by a negative vote. The content of this resolution is sound and should be supported. The other course which is open is to give this resolution some teeth; to make the government, the President of Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), the Public Service Commission and the Commissioner of Official Languages legally responsible for its implementation once it is accepted by this House. This is what the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition seeks to do. It sseks to turn the nine principles into law. Mr. Speaker, this amendment puts the government to the test: does it really mean what it says? Can it be trusted? Is it prepared to accept legal responsibility, as well as partisan political gain from a resolution which is so ill-timed and badly motivated?
Lest I be accused of making a purely political speech, let me suggest some advantages which would flow from the adoption of the amendment to make the nine points law. First, it would represent a much firmer direction to the government, the Treasury Board and the Public Service Commission to see that the principles and protections in this resolution are in fact applied. It would amount to parliament saying to these bodies: We mean business. You must have the bilingual positions identified and designated by December 31, 1978. You must open all competitions to unilingual candidates, French or English, who have formally indicated their willingness to become bilingual. You must protect the jobs of unilingual incumbents, even if their jobs become designated as bilingual. You must protect the promotion rights of all those in the civil service before 1966 with ten years experience, even if they are unwilling to become bilingual. You must provide effective language training where required.
By putting these and other principles and protections into law, you avoid putting Mr. Carson, Mr. Spicer and the President of Treasury Board into the invidious position of deciding between the enforcement of a statute having judicial sanction and the implementation of a mere resolution of the House of Commons, not having the force of law. The present resolution has no sanction in its provisions. Standing alone, it is merely a passive approval of certain measures with no power of disapprobation. Put into legislation, these difficulties would be overcome.
Second, the many thousands of persons having rights and duties under this resolution have no source of interpretation such as the courts, with respect to statutes. Various authorities may interpret the motion differently from one another and from occasion to occasion. Technically, the House of Commons would be the interpreter of its own resolution, and a person aggrieved by a decision of the authorities would have a remedy only by way of a petition to the House. But how workable would this be, considering the thousands of civil servants to be affected
Official Languages
by the provisions of the resolution? Surely it is better to put it into law, thus providing more certainty and uniformity in interpretation. This would apply particularly to decisions of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, arbitration tribunals and adjudicators hearing language grievances of federal employees under the relevant legislation.
Third, a final advantage relates to appeal rights. Last December, the President of Treasury Board promised the National Joint Council of the Public Service and Treasury Board that the government "was prepared to set up an appeal procedure if necessary". Yet the nine points contain nothing along these lines, and so far the government has not seen fit to make a specific proposal. By giving the nine points the force of law, as the amendment would do, we would increase the possibilities by which an aggrieved public servant, English or French, could pursue a remedy in the courts, whether by way of statutory appeal, right of review or prerogative writ.
An important new court, the Federal Court of Canada, was established by legislation in the last parliament. It permits easier access to a judicial remedy by persons aggrieved by decisions of federal boards, commissions or other tribunals. Regardless of the particular mode of access to the trial or appellate division of that court, which is now possible or would be possible under future amendments, it is certain that the principles and protections contained in the resolution before us will never represent a ground for going to court unless they are enacted into law. In their present state, however, they are impotent in the context of the judicial process.
What is the government's response to this amendment? The Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) spoke last Friday and ventured these observations: First, he said it was "amusing" that the opposition should favour actual legislation in the light of comments made prior to the passage of the Official Languages Act. Well, Mr. Speaker, we accepted that act. The Leader of the Official Opposition has crossed this country to obtain a broader understanding and compassion toward the act-a task often made much more difficult by the excesses, insults and indignities of the Trudeau government. It was not an "amusing" commitment which the Leader of the Opposition made them; nor is it, now, when he calls on the government to give the force of law to what it says. It was a deadly serious commitment.
Second, the Minister of Communications says that it would be extremely costly to go through the legislative process because it is quite painstaking. Surely, that statement alone proves the political motivation behind the resolution. The government really does not care enough to give the principles of protection the dignity of becoming law as long as it can achieve its political purposes. What would be the cost that would be so high? One would have thought that the government would have gained a little more respect for the legislative process since last October. I hope that the legislative process will not be treated as lightly as it has been. To refer to a comment made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that it is difficult to enact laws in this parliament; however, it may be easy to enact some important principles

June 5, 1973
Official Languages
into law and then have those principles implemented and applied through regulations, which are made, repealed, and then remade every day of the week.
Third, the Minister of Communications said that to amend the legislation would be a loss of time. A loss of time for what? The government is prepared to devote five days of House time at this point in our history to the discussion of a language resolution and to give it priority over housing legislation, tax legislation, family allowance legislation, much needed amendments to the Immigration Appeal Board Act-all matters of the utmost urgency. Yet it has the audacity to suggest to the House that the use of legislation to give added weight and certainty to the principles and protections would lead to a loss of time. This is hypocrisy of the highest order. The government wants the political benefits of the legislation but none of the responsibilities.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) rejected the amendment on behalf of the government because, he said, there must be flexibility. It seems strange that the Minister of Finance should make this argument now when in 1969, as Minister of Justice piloting the original bill through the House, he did not see any necessity for flexibility in regard to certain detailed and complex provisions relating to judicial proceedings which were contained in the Official Languages Act. He guided that act through the House and protected it against the onslaught of some provincial attorneys general.
These important provisions to which I have referred related to language rights of witnesses, simultaneous translation in the courts, and the language of proceedings in federal courts and in criminal cases in provincial courts. These were important provisions and protections which the government saw fit to include in its legislation. I am glad that the then minister of justice fought to put those protections into the legislation, even though some provincial attorneys general ultimately insisted that the protections be conditional upon provincial laws providing such protections in civil proceedings. The minister fought for those principles then and I only wish he would fight for them now. The protection afforded witnesses in the courts went into the law; why not protections afforded to the civil service?
To turn to the arguments made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, his reasons for not supporting the amendment are that the nine principles and related matters are still being sorted out. If they are still being sorted out, why does the government bring forward this resolution now? There are urgent items facing this House and the country, yet the government has seen fit to proceed with this resolution now. Surely, we have proceeded far enough and have sorted out sufficiently the principles and general statements now to go 100 per cent of the way.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that really we do need flexibility, again reiterating the argument made by the minister of justice.

speechtext:
Excuse me, the Minister of Finance. The hon. member said that the legislative process was a little too rigid for the task at hand. I do not need to tell the hon.

member of some of the devices available in legislation to overcome rigidity. Legislation has been enacted in this House in which provision is made that automatically, as of a certain date, the House or a committee of the House will undertake a review of its provisions. One also has other means of automatic termination or automatic review, committee screening or committee scrutiny, of particular pieces of legislation. The legislative process can be and has been part of the on-going process of consultation to which the hon. member referred, and which I agree is very important. So the government has flexibility even though it proceeds with legislation. I suggest the flexibility is there through the vehicle of regulations. Then, we have an important new joint committee of this House and the Senate known as the statutory instruments committee. It really has not done very much yet but I suggest it could perform a valuable function by reviewing the regulations, which are the traditional instruments of flexibility, and that the government should seriously consider this in this particular context.
I honestly urge members of the government, particularly the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Communications who are not here at the moment, to reconsider their objections to the amendment put forward by the Leader of the Opposition. I suggest that those objections are what might be termed "knee-jerk" reactions-automatic responses whenever the opposition proposes something positive. I candidly admit that sometimes the opposition, or individual members of the opposition, have "knee-jerk" reactions to government proposals; this is the very nature of the institution in which we are all working. But I think it would be in the interests of this country for the members of the government, and indeed the members of the party to my left, to reconsider their position seriously, to examine the resolution before us and to ask themselves whether they agree with us that it should be given teeth by being incorporated into law.
Let me conclude by touching on broader items but within the context of the language question. I agree with others in this House who have said that this government has made a fundamental mistake in its approach to language rights. In my view, this fundamental mistake is that it sees protection of language rights as the only solution to problems in Canada. It is an approach which concentrates only upon institutional values and ignores more fundamental claims to economic and social equality which can only be achieved through more effective policies relating to prices, incomes, social services and regional disparities, policies certainly more effective than the government has provided to date.
This simple, straight-line approach of the present government ignores the fact that man's salvation, whether he be a francophone, an anglophone, or a member of a third linguistic group, is not merely to have services from his government in his own language; that is only part of the problem. Too often we look at the provision of government services as the cure-all. Surely, it is equally important, if not more important, to ensure that the individual has a climate of freedom-freedom to seek a job or vocation, freedom to travel, to join organizations, to read, to earn a decent living, to have decent housing, to develop himself spiritually and intellectually, and to gain the respect and admiration of his fellow man. These are some of the goals
June 5, 1973

of Canadians whatever their language. Language is important. But language claims often tend to be outward manifestations of more basic human claims made as a result of a wide range of social, economic and cultural deprivations. Let us get on with the task of meeting some of the problems faced by this country. The principles of the language resolution will help, but they are not the only solution to national unity. Most Canadians agree with these principles; let us pass them now. I would be happier to enact them into law, but regardless, let us pass them and get on to other things. There is so much to do; let us get on with the job.
I should like in this debate to associate myself with the thoughtful remarks of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Official Opposition and even the leader of the NDP. These are the true leaders of this country, the people to whom the great majority of Canadians look for guidance, leadership and direction. Most important of all, these are the leaders of the young people of this country who have articulated their goals and their aspirations. Young Canadians want many things in relation to language; they want educational support to the provinces for second-language training. Sometimes they wish the government would do a better job of explaining its bilingual policy to their parents and grandparents, as this would mean their goals and aspirations might be easier met. Most of all, young Canadians will support this resolution and its contents, whatever its form, so let us get on with the job.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my remarks with a quotation from the B and B Royal Commission report. Paragraph 243 read thus:
The possibility of national disintegration has forced a reexamination of the linguistic policies of the Public Service. The debate is no longer about efficiency, merit, patronage, and representation, but rather between thorough-going reform and schism.
"Reform or schism", that is indeed the subject of the debate we are holding these days. Some complain, and I understand them, about this matter being brought up, it is of course a subject which arouses passions and reveal plainly the prejudicies of a good part of our population.
However, in my opinion, we will have to settle this question once and for all because as a great historian said in a book entitled Maple Leaf Forever the story of this country has always been unstable and precarious precisely because our major problems have never been discussed and never been settled at the satisfaction of our two great majorities.
When you read the report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism whose members were chosen among our most competent citizens and when you see at each page the injustice inflicted upon our Frenchspeaking people you cannot but feel frustrated and I would say you cannot help crying over such small results achieved after 100 years.
I would quote only a few pertinent paragraphs. Paragraph 730 reads as follows:
730. On balance, however-
Official Languages -despite all the progress made-[DOT]
-extensive optimism is not warranted. In an organizational structure where the English language and culture predominate, there are still many factors blocking the progress of Francophones.
The three most important involve their adjustment to settings where English is dominant, their aversion to making geographic moves outside French-speaking areas,-
-and this is understandable-
-and problems of social relations and sponsorship.
I now quote from paragraph 752:
Everywhere in the Public Service there is great concern for recruiting Francophones, but the desire seems to be for men who will fit easily into the existing structure. The desire for Francophones was rarely complemented by a willingness to provide the intellectual atmosphere and working conditions for the development of their talents-The greatest drawback Francophone public servants must face is the cultural milieu of the federal administration: it is so overwhelmingly "English" that it is difficult for Francophones to identify with its problems or with the style of life, honour, and prestige of its officers.
I now quote from paragraph 767:
The greatest obstacle to equal partnership in the federal Public Service-The factor that most impedes a strong Francophone presence is the environment of the Public Service: its underlying assumptions and conventions, its prejudices, and, most important, its language, all of which are overwhelming of English-speaking Canada.
The discrimination of which the French-speaking population has been the victim had been exposed some years before by the Glassco Commission which was set up by the official opposition and had been made known much earlier by the French-speaking group since the beginning of the century. Let us remember the Lacroix amendment, the Jean committee, the amendments proposed by the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, and all the committees set up in the past: we see that progress has been slow, that the French Canadians have suffered from injustice and that the resolution before the House is in my opinion a very small effort to remedy the situation.
Some maintain that the Official Languages Act has settled those problems. Let me emphasize what the Commissioner of Official Languages wrote, a few weeks ago, in the report submitted to the House. On page 12, we can read and I quote:
Although the Act has been in effect for well over three years, it is painfully clear that many government agencies still consider the Act part of a distant and irrelevant archive. As a result, they have too often proven unwilling-
In the legal sense, unwilling and malice are the same thing, Mr. Speaker.
-or unable to effect significant reform without the Commissioner's intervention.
And he quotes several examples, particularly on page 9, some of which are shocking.
And that is why many French Canadians-myself included-are being humiliated every day in Ottawa because of the way they are treated as French Canadians and that is why I am not surprised when French-speaking public servants come to me and say that they can no longer live in such a hostile environment and prefer to go back to the province of Quebec.

June 5, 1973
Official Languages
And that humiliation, once again, is an every day reality, and many examples could be given merely on the way the French language is respected even here within the walls of this Parliament.
I just mentioned the alienation of French-speaking public servants. One could talk about the alienation of English-speaking westerners who are no more adequately represented in the federal public service. One could also talk in passing about the alienation of English-speaking Quebecers who are absent from the provincial public service. One can also talk about the absence of native groups. But I know that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) is making considerable efforts in that respect within his department. I was speaking a while ago of alienation English-speaking westerners who are also right when they complain, because in a federal government, a government that should represent citizens from all Canada, all areas-maritimes provinces or Quebec or western Canada-should be represented as Ontario has always been.
My other comment is that considering all the efforts that were made during the last half-century, the amendments to the regulations of the Public Service Commission, the laws that were enacted and the resolutions that remained a dead letter, I believe it is high time we had a control system as they say in English a monitoring system-to check the progress that will be made.
The resolution mentions efforts to appoint Frenchspeaking people. I could quote regulations going as far back as 1908, about efforts in that, field. One needs only recall the right hon. Lester B. Pearson, the hon. Maurice Lamontagne and many other leaders who also talked about efforts to appoint French-speaking people. Moreover, let me recall that in 1955 the number of Francophones in the public service amounted to 22 per cent and that this percentage has not increased since. I believe that a close supervision will be necessary to make sure that there is progress.
And to think that more than 65 big statistical charts were prepared by the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission and that not a single one was kept up to date, while we know very well that statistics on almost everything in Canada, except this question, were of some concern-one might say that to talk about that is inelegant, disgraceful or improper-I think that work will have to be done over again and kept up to date.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the fate of the French-speaking group in this country for the last 100 years does not speak well for us; it is not one of the most beautiful pages in the history of this country. Not only are we a minority submerged in an English-speaking environment, but everything has worked against us.
I do not wish to go back very far, but let us consider only the immigration policy for the past 100 years. Nothing has been done during the past 100 years to prevent immigration from jeopardizing further the dangerous position of the French-Canadian people.
Finally, as to the measure for the establishment of French language units, I think that the only model acceptable is that suggested by the commission, especially on pages 284 and the following of the report, where it spells

out what are French language units, that is a department where, parallel to unilingual English language units, we would have an equally important unilingual French language section in addition to common bilingual services. It is different from what we have now where French units, for all practical purposes, are located in certain parts of Quebec.
It is not surprising, Mr. Speaker, in view of the situation I have just described, that we should notice that the percentage of resignations and departures among Frenchspeaking Canadians is, according to the statistics of the commission, much greater than among English-speaking Canadians. I think it is true that they cannot indefinitely bear this alienation to which they are submitted every day and eventually they leave the federal civil service.
I think that we should fight on a daily basis. Most of our past efforts have led to failures. We failed to make this country really the true champion of both cultures. Mr. Speaker, far from me the idea of uttering threats, but my humble opinion is that the separation of Quebec from the rest of Canada is written down in history unless we succeed in making Ottawa and the federal government the champion of the two cultures. And to the extent where French Canadians will feel humiliated as they still do today, I think that this is the most dangerous seed for separation.
Obviously, it can be said that I am exaggerating, just as French Canadians said that English-Canadian westerners exaggerated when they complained when someone suggested doing away with the four small letters R.C.M.P. But this reminds me of a sentence by Albert Memmi in his book "Le portrait d'un homme colonise": "When someone complains about the injustice he is suffering from, he is always told that he exaggerates".
Mr. Speaker, during the five years I have been here, I have too often witnessed the humiliation the French Canadians are suffering from. I live with it every day and I say that the issues of poverty or economic disparities or others are not at the root of the need French Canadians have to separate, to assert themselves, but it is this constant humiliation in which they are held.
Insofar as I am concerned, it is a daily tragedy to live in an environment which is, not hostile, but unaware of our dignity, and I say to myself that were the English-speaking Canadians to suffer the same prejudices, they would not tolerate them either.
This country is made of two majorities, and together they can form a country where we can really offer to the world an example of tolerance and civilization.
Otherwise, it must be remembered that the Frenchspeaking Canadians have a territory of their own, that they have their own government, and if they are humiliated further, it would be most easy for them, overnight, to find a way to live in dignity.
Mr. Speaker, I am here to fight, to keep this country united, but I hope that everyone in this House will want to face this problem once and for all. All our statistics prove what the two Royal Commissions of inquiry and the present Chairman of the Public Service Commission have denounced, including the "discrimination" against the French-Canadians over the past few years.
June 5, 1973

It is important to recognize this and to take the necessary steps to keep our country united. Of course, this will mean concerted efforts and a high price; but it all this depends upon our scale of values. Do we want a united country or not? If the effort is really too great, let us say so. If economic values must have priority, we might as well join the United States. However, I have always thought that we stood for other values and, in this respect, to my mind the co-existence of various groups within the same community bears witness to a civilized society. It is pointless to dream of understanding between men, between peoples of the world who have never met if, in this country, where we have been living side by side for the past 100 years, we cannot achieve more mutual respect.
Mr. Speaker, a debate such as this one today is essential. It must be devoid of political considerations. I mentioned earlier, and other hon. members repeated it after me, that it has been said that it is indecent to speak of co-existence between various groups which have never gone to the roots of these problems; I, for one, consider that it is imperative that we talk about it now, if we do not want to face separatist and secessionist winds later on.
Mr. Speaker, we must recognize, as the Royal Commission on bilingualism and biculturalism stressed on every page of its report, the problem of the federal administration; as we can read in every paragraph of Volume III, it is the problem of discrimination against French Canadians. Let us read again all its recommendations; every one is related to the discrimination against Francophones.
That is why I wish I could have voted for the amendment moved by the Leader of the official opposition (Mr. Stanfield), but, unfortunately, this amendment relates only to the first part of the resolution. I really don't understand why it cannot also include the second part of the resolution, which is a follow-up, a reply to the Commission's report.
This is, Mr. Speaker, what I had to say. I think that coolly and dispassionately we will have to tackle the problem as it is, that of a people who for 100 years have been denied justice. Surely there has been some progress, but as they assert themselves increasingly, and become aware that they must shape their own fate, two avenues are open to them; either, become equal partners, and I think that it is the only valid objective in the federal Public Service, or entrench themselves. We must all cooperate so that those two large groups, as well as all the others which have been unfairly treated, may feel fairly dealt with by the Canadian government. To the extent where the government or the entire country become defenders of the French as well as the English cultures- and that is the only solution-this problem will be solved. Any other procedure or solution is a palliative that will not stand the test of time and the awareness of the people.
That is why I think that this debate should be held on a higher level than that of politics; the time has come to make the same diagnosis as the Commission and say that the only possible solution for this country is to act so both majorities will consider themselves as equal partners.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the speaker who just resumed his seat. I believe he spoke as a real French Canadian; he deserves our consideration.
I have read very carefully the resolution moved by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) concerning the use of both official languages within the Public Service. My speech will certainly not be as well structured and as colorful as the one made by the right hon. Prime Minister as I do not have the multiplicity of 90 per cent Englishspeaking technocrats who surround him to think and write for him, as is also the case with the Treasury Board President (Mr. Drury).
In fact, as I have said already in this House, that deep feeling of discomfort that exists in this parliament is due to the fact that the government is only the reflection of the bureaucracy-in the main, Anglophone-that reigned supreme over all successive governments.
In such a government, the minister, as well as the government member, completely loses his personality. That explains, in fact, why voters no longer recognize their representatives once they sit on the government side.
As, for 11 years now, I have made it a point of being realistic, I may be harsh towards some, but I intend, even so, to tell you the truth about bilingualism in the Public Service as well as in our federal courts of justice and Crown corporations. As I am not in power, I do not have to act according to the pleasure of a dictatorial bureaucracy and I can voice the views of the people.
In order to hide their incapacity to change anything basic, the government members, who have succeeded one another during 100 years of confederative life, have tossed around beautiful principles without ever achieving any concrete results.
The resolution introduced in the House on May 30 last is an unparalleled example of what I have just stated. At the beginning, it is the same old story, that is the principles concerning the official languages embodied indefinitely in Chapter 0-2 of Volume V of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1970.
Naturally, we are for those principles since we have adopted them, but we are for their implementation and not for their shelving. Mr. Speaker, here is the beginning of the resolution of the right hon. Prime Minister as given on page 4302 of Hansard:

That this House,
(i) aware that, as provided in the Official Languages Act, the English and French languages possess and enjoy equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all the institutions of the Parliament and Government of Canada; cognizant that it is the duty of departments and agencies of the Government of Canada to ensure, in accordance with that Act, that members of the public can obtain available services from and communicate with them in both official languages; while recognizing that public servants should, as a general proposition and subject to the requirements of the Official Languages Act respecting the provision of services to the public, be able to carry out their duties in the Public Service of Canada in the official language of their choice;
do hereby recognize and approve the following Principles for achieving the foregoing:

June 5, 1973
Official Languages
And following that hymn to the glory of the principles, the Prime Minister makes an extraordinary discovery. He discovers the reality of the country. After having repeated his song on national unity, he finds out that we are dealing with specific political and social realities. And I quote again the Prime Minister:
We are dealing with very specific political and social realities.
And a stark reality of our country is this: there are about 16 million English-speaking Canadians, most of whom speak no French. There are about 6 million French-speaking Canadians, a majority of whom speak no English. If only because of sheer force of numbers, either group has the power to destroy the unity of this country.
Those are the facts, Mr. Speaker: two numerically dominant language groups, both of them prevalently unilingual. As the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) reminded us last December:
That same President of the Treasury Board repeated that to us in his last speech which completed the one written for the Prime Minister. Nevertheless, I want to warn the persons in charge at the office of the President of the Treasury Board about contradictions, when they state on page 4347 of the Hansard, and I quote:
It is part of this law that Canadians should be able to receive services from, and communicate with, their government in the official language of their choice.
That conditional mood, Mr. Speaker, well indicates that all Canadians do not now have that power to communicate, even after the passing of the Official Languages Act.
Why then does he state in the same paragraph, and I quote:
In Canada . . . the passage of the Official Languages Act made this the law.
Even if one is a seasoned civil servant, one need not treat everybody like morons.
I was also very much interested by the speech of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield)-which easily harmonizes with the statements of the Prime Minister-although his predecessor was singing a different tune.
I was very much impressed by the frankness of the Leader of the Official Opposition who stated that this motion, which he will nevertheless support, is null and void. We can read his statement in Hansard on page 4314, where the Leader of the Official Opposition is reported as saying:
The adoption of this resolution-I emphasize this-is not binding on the government. It is a matter of law, despite what the Prime Minister said in the House of May 7 of this year in answer to the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). One might argue, of course, that there would be some moral obligation on the part of the government to comply with the resolution, but there certainly could be no legal obligation on the part of the government, or officials administering the legislation, because this resolution cannot have the force of law, cannot change any existing law and cannot be binding upon those who are administering the law.
One realizes that the civil servants who hold positions are reassured. They will never be subjected to any obligations. That is a point which the Prime Minister strove to hide from the House, for fear of informing the Canadian people.

When the Official Languages Act was promulgated, it was evident that many civil servants were afraid of some transfers. When, after nearly 100 years, during which the public service was open only to unilingual English-speaking Canadians and a few perfectly bilingual Frenchspeaking Canadians, it was quite difficult for this predominating group to accept the arrival of a group which represents after all one third of the Canadian population. And I am quite moderate when I say this, since the Leader of the New Democratic Party, who can speak freely to the English-speaking people, stated in the House on May 31, and I quote:
Those of us who are English-speaking and who see that side ought to remember that the French-speaking Canadian has not had an opportunity to advance in the public service of Canada, not only for a century but for two centuries: not only since confederation, but for a century before confederation that was the situation in this country.
Those are statements which speak volumes and at the same time explain the reaction of the young people, particularly in Quebec, when they see such absurd and longstanding discrimination. Indeed, when the young people look at all the efforts made by the Creditistes since 1962 in order to be recognized as French Canadians, more specifically in this House, they cannot but be disappointed to realize the few gains painfully acquired.
An English-speaking member was pleased to praise the simultaneous translation now available in this House as well as in committees. But do the members newly elected since 1962 even know about the fight that we, of the Creditiste party, had to put up to get that service in all the standing committees of the House.
Mr. Speaker, I still remember as if it were yesterday all the sarcasm and the insults we had to put up with from our fellow citizens, some of whom were French-speaking. The latter called us "peasants" and "stupid" because we dared protest against English-speaking unilinguism which had always existed in committees.
At that time, at the end of our tether, in order to have few words of French in committees, we finally decided to boycott committee work until we obtained justice. The operation was successful because since then, we enjoy this marvelous system of simultaneous translation.
I frankly admit that many times I felt like giving up everything because of the attitude of my French-speaking colleagues who sat on those committees. And had it not been for the support of many of my English-speaking friends, some of whom are still in the House today and I could point at, I believe that we could not survive those insidious attacks.
Indeed, when we left the committee rooms after stopping any proceedings without interpretation, those sincere friends whom I will never forget even if they were not from my party, shaked hands with me and said, "Cheer up, you will win. Pay no attention to your fellow countrymen, only think of your cause, because you are one hundred per cent right."
Today, we hear those jokers, those third rate members who fought against us during those difficult years, say in the House that their party introduced the simultaneous translation and that they granted some other small concessions to French Canadians. They seem satisfied with the
June 5, 1973

crumbs obtained after much protest and pleading. It is because of such jokers that Quebec has never managed to take its place within the Canadian nation.
Let us stop saying "damned Englishmen" and let us look at ourselves in the mirror in order to see if we truly reflect the image ascribed to us by the people in Quebec. We have just conducted a little investigation on the percentage of French Canadians within the public service. And yet there are many French-Canadian ministers in the present cabinet. It is simply revolting, Mr. Speaker, to think that we make up one third of the population of Canada and that new Canadians outnumber us in the public service. Nevertheless, French Canadians in other parties say they are satisfied with the situation.
The Prime Minister boasts about being a dyed-in-the-wool French Canadian, but he has not dared yet hire a single unilingual French Canadian, whereas 90 per cent of his battalion is made up of unilingual anglophones, the few French Canadians working for him being all fluently bilinguals. "How about that?" as the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) would say.
In another area, the National Energy Board and the Treasury Board Secretariat answered a question from the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin) concerning the percentage of English-speaking and French-speaking civil servants. As far as the National Energy Board is concerned, out of 212 employees, 173 are unilingual anglophones, 1 is francophone and 38 are bilingual. At the Treasury Board Secretariat, out of 159 employees, 126 are unilingual anglophones, there are no francophones and 33 are bilingual.
As a result, I think the figures speak for themselves! We do not need any other proof. I said I would throw some light on some truths that honest Canadians will find shocking, but they must be told in this House. It is all very well to buy "translating machines", but what about the increase in the number of French-speaking employees here in Parliament? May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying at six o'clock, it is all very well to have bought and installed a simultaneous translation system, but the increase in the number of francophones in the Public Service of Canada must also be accelerated, mainly, at the higher levels of administration. As a matter of fact, I have found that it is extremely difficult for a French-Canadian, even if he is bilingual, to have precedence over an unilingual anglophone. What happens to the 7 per cent bonus for bilingualism designed for the bilingual employees? There again, some cards are not played according to the rules of the game. If I had the time to do so, I would mention hundreds of cases where people complained of discrimina-
Official Languages
tion to my office, in Parliament, and that I was able to look into. But, what can we do? We run up against a wall of silence at the higher levels of the Civil Service. Everything is done so silently that even the Members of Parliament can't break this silence.
I heard the Leader of the NDP say that this resolution should not have been brought before the House. In this regard, may I be permitted to quote his statement which is recorded in Hansard of May 31, 1973. And I quote:
In a sense, I regret that this resolution has been brought before the House, not for some of the reasons I have heard but for another and perhaps deeper reason.
I have learned that in life, particularly in collective life, there are matters with respect to which repeated argument produces confrontation and repeated confrontation pollutes rather than clears the air-
-I am not certain that it is the wisest step to bring this resolution before the House.
A statement was made by the late Mr. Pearson with regard to policies in the public service. That was followed by the adoption of the Official Languages Act, supported by all parties in this House. Some members opposed it, but all parties officially supported it. We had the introduction of new public service suggestions after volume 3 of the B and B report. Commissioner Spicer reported twice to this Parliament. There has been a great deal of discussion on the subject across this country.
One of the disturbing things about this kind of delicate, sensitive subject is that instead of discussion producing more understanding and clearing the air, it frequently rejuvenates prejudices and misunderstandings rather than allaying them. That is why I am sorry to some extent that this resolution is now before us.
The leader of the New Democratic Party seems to be afraid of delicate and sensitive subjects as he calls them. Well, we are not afraid of them at all, because we know how to deal with thorny subjects. You just have to pluck off their thorns.
That is why we are going to consider carefully the nine principles contained in the Prime Minister's resolution. Let me warn hon. members right away that even though we agree with the introduction and the conclusion of this resolution, we are strongly opposed to some items because they counteract the beneficial effects of the resolution itself.
The first principle reads as follows:
that positions which are seen, under present circumstances, as requiring the knowledge and use of both the French and English languages will be first identified, and then designated, as bilingual in the course of the period ending December 31, 1978;
We cannot accept to wait another five years after having already lost four. Indeed, since the act was promulgated, nothing has been done. People seemed convinced that it was only a matter of passing an act and that everything would go well in the public service. And as a consolation prize, the Prime Minister tells us that bilingual positions will be identified within a period of five years. It is that extension, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot accept.
The second principle reads as follows:
that positions will also be identified where English is an essential requirement of the job, where French is essential, or whether either French or English may be used;

June 5, 1973
Official Languages
That falls precisely within our principles of letting each citizen decide freely on those positions, French positions and English positions.
The third principle deals with standard knowledge, and I quote:
that a knowledge of English and French is one of the elements of merit in the selection of candidates for bilingual positions;
And I read it purposely because the next principle contradicts this last one when it is says that knowledge of French and English is absolutely essential to be able to seek bilingual positions.
As for the fourth principle, we read in connection with competitions, and I quote:
(4)	competitions for bilingual positions will be open both to bilingual candidates and unilingual candidates-
A bilingual position is set up and will be open to unilingual candidates-
-who have formally indicated their willingness to become bilingual;
It is somewhat as if we started to give a doctor's degree to a student wishing to become a doctor. It seems to me quite normal to require qualifications from someone for a competition. But everything is turned upside down with this resolution saying that unilingual candidates will also be eligible for competitions for bilingual positions.
The fifth principle reads as follows:
(5)	that competitions for unilingual positions will continue to be open to unilingual or bilingual candidates who meet the language requirements of the job;
This is quite well, we admit it.
The sixth principle is as follows: that unilingual incumbents-
I think that the Prime Minister felt remorse when he included that principle in his resolution.
(6)	that unilingual incumbents of bilingual positions may elect to become bilingual and undertake language training, or transfer to another job having the same salary maximum, or, if they were to decline such a transfer, to remain-
-simply in their position, not give a darn about bilingualism and continue to practise unilingualism just as in the two past centuries.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this provision is a backward step; we will prevent those who are qualified from holding positions which they would fill better than unilingual individuals. I continue the quotation dealing further with unilingualism:
(7)	that employees who, as of April 6, 1966, had at least ten years of continuous service and who, since that date, have been employed continuously in the federal Public Service, will be entitled to apply for any job-
... let us not forget that we are always referring to unilingual employees ...
. .. that has been identified for future designation as bilingual without having to indicate their willingness to become bilingual;
It is fantastic, Mr. Speaker. The worse is still to come:
(8)	that unilingual French-speaking and English-speaking persons from outside the Public Service ...
... who have never worked in the Public Service . . .
. .. who are willing to become bilingual may apply for bilingual positions . ..
Imagine the mess! And they will try to make us swallow that!
I frankly say, after reading those conditions, that it is impossible for us to remain unconcerned about those proposals which are a complete reversal of the idea which underlies the preamble to the resolution.
The Prime Minister suggests at first the establishment of bilingual positions to guarantee adequate service to both main ethnic groups in Canada, but those positions may be filled by unilingual employees. The only qualification required will be the desire to learn another language. Nobody may be compelled to learn another language.
When bilingual districts and bilingual positions have been set up by the government, several persons, including our young university graduates who are perfectly bilingual, will be ready to take over. We will then have a sufficient number of competent people to fill those positions without being obliged to submit ourselves to the principles included in this resolution which are "superlatively ridiculous" because it will have been pointless for the Prime Minister to arrive at such brilliant conclusions and then destroy them completely by imposing politically biased conditions. This is mainly the result of political fears: the liberals have not yet admitted their last defeat; they will resort to anything to get votes from our two main ethnic groups in the next election.
Although the first principles of the resolution are good, the three or four I have mentioned are quite bad and unacceptable to my colleagues of the Social Credit.
Here is the only solution: If we want everyone to be satisfied, two parallel systems should be established, one in French and the other in English. This will be costly, but not more than all the bilingual positions that will never be bilingual and that will always be English unilingual. The only way to work towards national unity and to meet the needs of both groups in the linguistic field is to accept the proposals made recently by my colleague for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) and by the other members of the Social Credit, namely to create two parallel groups within the Public Service, one English and the other French.
Thus, we will really be able to strive towards national unity within diversity. Because Canada is unity within diversity, let us respect this diversity and give each citizen what he needs to live and guarantee his language and his institutions.
Then we will start working seriously towards Canadian unity.

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by extending my congratulations to the hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane) who spoke this afternoon and to tell him, through you, Sir, that I appreciated the forthright and sincere manner of his speech and hope that he will accept mine in the same spirit.

June 5, 1973

I rise as a western Canadian to take part briefly in this debate. No one can presume to speak for all of western Canada; it is a huge expanse of diverse interests and a multitude of cultures. It is this very variety that is one of our strengths. But we consider ourselves Canadian first and we put the interests of Canada ahead of regional viewpoints. At least, that is the approach of those for whom I speak in this House. With great deference to those who pioneered those great open spaces, with great respect to those who claim an affinity to languages and cultures other than English and French, we speak for the new west.
It is time for Canada to hear the voice of the new west. We are urban and up to date. We are cosmopolitan, with the virtues and vices found in central Canada. We have skyscrapers and traffic jams, cuisine and culture and computers; and lots of energy, both in the ground and in the bodies of industrious, ambitious people. In short, we have the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of Canadians everywhere. We want justice for ourselves, just as we are ready to do our part to obtain justice for all racial and ethnic groups in Canada.
The new west, then-and let this be heard clearly across the land-supports the principles of the Official Languages Act of 1969. Perhaps it was hard at first to swallow, because of our affinity with so many languages other than French, but the new west knows that it was a federal partnership of English and French which created Canada and we respect the principle that the future of one Canada, our Canada, depends on the maintenance of that partnership of equality.

Today, the Western provinces welcome the participation of the French-speaking Quebecers at the governmental level, and after hearing the points made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) on bilingualism among federal employees, nobody can question the issue of this discussion.
As the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is suggesting, the resolution should be annexed to the act, thus making it legal, and ensuring equal protection to all civil servants French- or English-speaking.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
The amendment put forward by my hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), is a move to secure both justice and solidarity. It is the Leader of the Opposition who has provided the real leadership on this issue. Mr. Speaker, this spirit of justice and scrupulous concern for the rights of public servants is applauded by the new west. We know that if the government had been led in the past five years by that honest man from Nova Scotia, we in the west would not have felt humiliated by the downgrading of the monarchy, the diminution of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the gestures of contempt at the hands of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
It is lack of concern for our feelings and traditions that has exacerbated the acceptance of functional bilingualism. People in the west have felt threatened that government would be shut off from them unless they spoke French. It was the overbearing manner of the government that
Official Languages
aroused fears in people and created resentment. If the nine points introduced by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and the uplifting demeanour of the Prime Minister last Thursday had been in evidence these past few years, Canada would have been more at peace with itself, and the personal crises experienced by many in the civil service who felt their careers being peremptorily jeopardized could have been avoided.
I understand that the resolution before us protects the careers of unilingual public servants, whether they speak English or French, while at the same time guaranteeing services to the public in both languages. That demonstrates fairness, and I support it. L. W. Barnes, executive director of the Professional Institute of Canada, the certified bargaining agent for 38 professional groups in the public service, has said that the guidelines in this resolution represent a "great improvement". Claude Edwards, president of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, said the guidelines meet most of his objectives.
Let us not, therefore, debate endlessly a resolution that is good for Canada. In Mr. Keith Spicer we have a language ombudsman and I am confident that if we adopt the approach reflected in his second annual report we will make progress. Of course, in matters of bilingualism and multiculturalism a sense of good will and trust is essential. I want the people of Quebec to know that the new west offers that good will and trust.
Education, as everyone knows, is the key to bilingualism. It is in the kindergartens and primary grades that we can make the most significant contribution to developing linguistic fluency; that is where our money and efforts should be directed. English-French relations must be constantly improved for the good of our country. Let us end the two solitudes and work together to build a Canada that yearns to fulfil its destiny in the new global society. Statesmanship, not diatribe, is what this chamber needs and the country wants. I am proud to support the statesmanship of the Leader of the Opposition whose speech on national unity last Thursday was the finest moment the twenty-ninth parliament has yet seen.
Let those who would sow suspicions be trampled in a new harvest of national unity in which the rights of all Canadians are protected and fostered. Let us strive for a new level of national unity, conscious that the aged, youth, women, as well as language groups, must be able to plug into our society.
All this is what the new west wants. Our Canada is on a broad canvas. We have no time for narrow fixations or old battles. We want to spend our energies solving the economic and social problems facing us. In the west we have brains, energy and good will, and we will not be deflected from our task. I say to hon. members: "Let us get on with the job of helping all Canadians achieve their levels of greatness.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take long in expressing my views on this subject. I do not believe that anything I might say would greatly influence other members, since I am sure this question has been on their minds for a considerable time and they have

June 5, 1973
Official Languages
already reached a conclusion as to the way in which they intend to vote.
I want to say a few words about the resolution, and I should like to say this at the outset. This is a very sensitive issue. A person's language, or mother tongue as it were, is so much part of his own personality, his family inheritance and background, that it is very difficult to deal with the subject in a large context. On a personal basis it is quite simple, because in personal, individual discussions one can show respect to another human being and this foreshadows, or should foreshadow, any background experiences of individuals involved in such kinds of personal relationships.
However, when government makes a formal decision with regard to the language issue the situation becomes more difficult to cope with, or to appreciate or understand what is involved. The course upon which any government sets out in dealing with language and linguistic matters is impeded by a large number of hazards, not the least of which are emotional feelings that stem from a person's childhood, his upbringing, his schooling and his associations in early life. Not the least of these emotional feelings are those concerning a person's current status if he feels his job or security is threatened either in a real or imagined way.
This is because government is generally insensitive to an individual's plight or his concerns. Government is too big, too massive an organization-and so are big companies-to be aware of any emotional sensitivities that a person has if his job is in jeopardy as a result of linguistic policy. The same is true if his stature in society is placed in doubt, or the way he grew up in life is threatened. In this regard, and for these reasons, I think that government has to be extra careful when dealing with such matters. It has to tread softly and carefully and to move tentatively when bringing about any alteration to existing language concepts within this nation.
Regrettably, I suppose, from the point of view of national unity about which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his government like to speak so often, the Liberal party has not as a government trodden softly. In fact, if anything it has trampled heavily in the area of language. This government has become associated with the imposition of language upon the public service, particularly with the imposition of the French language upon people in the public service who have worked for many years in a unilingual, English-speaking capacity. On the other hand, one can say this is only the reverse of the coin so far as the Quebecois are concerned, because for four years the English language has been imposed upon French-speaking people from and in Quebec. As I understand it, there has been a denial of opportunity in the past for people of French-speaking origin to move freely, especially in government circles.
However, I do not think that this has been the result of any deliberate or conscious act imposed by statute law or by declaration by the Parliament of Canada; it has resulted from natural outgrowth within the province of Quebec itself. This outgrowth in turn arose from the attitude taken by the late Premier Duplessis, who to my mind was

very parochial in outlook and anti-Canadian in view. He rejected any concept of federalism, rejected aid for universities, refused to accept grants for the trans-Canada highway, as well as a whole bunch of other things designed to assist in the development and growth of Canada as national policy. This outgrowth probably also sprang from an educational system that was geared largely to matters that were neither governmental nor economic but which were largely connected with the arts, and so on. So it is a question of trying to balance the books.
I do not like the term "French Canadian" although it is used pretty commonly, but there are many people of French-speaking origin who during the few years that I have been a member of this House have increasingly, and I think rightly, been demanding respect for themselves, for their language and their position. While it is true that they deserve respect in this regard, it is equally true that they themselves must also show respect. While there may be bigots of great stature, according to their own designation, both in this House and elsewhere of English-speaking background, there are also, regrettably, people of Frenchspeaking origin who are equally bigoted in their view of people of English descent.
A very sad moment in the consideration of the language question came about when the Prime Minister entered into the throne speech debate last January and gave what I would call, in the most polite terms I can think of, a terrible example of indiscretion so far as the language question is concerned. I think he did as much at that time to indicate that he had a closed mind on this subject as others who have spoken in the last day or so in this House have done.
What the speech of the Prime Minister did was to indicate that in January he and some of his colleagues were not really desirous of showing generosity in regard to the development of bilingualism within the public service. His was a comment that was made out of pique. His was a reaction and a response to something that took place on October 30 last, namely, the election. I do not want to dwell too long on that matter because it is an insignificant part of what I want to say.
By contrast, I think we also saw the other side of the Jekyll and Hyde personality that comprises the Prime Minister of this nation. In introducing the resolution to this House he was extremely contrite. He was sorry and rather reflective about his past errors and sins, which showed, I think, not a change in substance or in attitude per se but at least a change in technique and in approach.
Earlier, outside the House, I had expressed the thought that the Prime Minister was a bit childish in wanting to bring a resolution of this nature before the House and to test the authority of his government upon that resolution in terms of want of confidence. I said that if he had wanted an election based on the linguistic policy of the government, there would have been many people in this House, I for one, who would have been glad to accommodate him. But because I felt that the Prime Minister was childish and wrong in his approach is no reason why I have to be.
I am trying to assess as objectively as possible what the initial dangers are that exist in respect of the Official
June 5, 1973

Languages Act and its application to the resolution before us. I think there is great danger in trying to equate bilingualism with Canadian unity. The feeling of Canadians for this nation goes far beyond the question of the linguistic background of an individual or the lack of it, and to try to suggest that one is equal to the other is extremely dangerous.
There is a danger in attempting to bring into effect a policy of bilingualism or any policy of that nature. There is a danger in attempting to force upon Canadians any policy that touches upon Canadian unity. Surely it is dangerous to bring in any policy with the suggestion that the future of this country depends upon its acceptance- and that is the attitude of the government in respect of bilingualism. There is the suggestion that if bilingualism is not accepted, the future of Canada is likewise unacceptable and will fail.
This policy of bilingualism within the public service is a marked change from the attitude exhibited last year by the government. There is a tremendous amount of jealousy among various levels of the public service. There is a great hiving for positions by members of the public service solely for the purpose of advancement, increased power and less work. Many of these people are very narrow minded. There has been, there is and still can be an attitude on the part of certain individuals in the public service to force linguistic requirements on people who may well be at the lower levels of the public service.

What distresses me more is the fear that now exists among English-speaking people. The French unilingual knows he has the support of the government behind him. speechtext:
I am sad because we as Canadians are losers again. In the throne speech the government preached two priorities, the first about economic matters and the second about social and welfare matters. Neither priority has been established to any degree in this parliament. Canadians have been fooled again. This government has falsely presented the facts, and I call this a misrepresentation. They have changed the list of priorities. I am also saddened because lurking in the background is Canadian unity.
In May and June of 1968 in the constituency which I have the privilege and honour to represent, namely, Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton, one could see a sign on all the trees and telegraph poles which read "One Canada: Trudeau, McBride". In 1969 a language debate took place and my Liberal predecessor did not take part in it, I am informed by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), because he felt that his constituents did not want him to speak in support of the Official Languages Act. I do not hide. I will speak in favour of the Official Languages Act and of this resolution.
In 1972, after the election of October 30, I was somewhat discouraged and disappointed in my predecessor, the Reverend Murray McBride, referring to the people in Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton as bigots, as was reported from coast to coast and appeared on the front pages of Vancouver newspapers and Halifax newspapers. This is the man who did not have the courage to speak in the debate on the Official Languages Act, yet he called us bigots.
In January of 1973 I almost rose in my place for the first time on a question of privilege when the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was addressing this House and made a comment which could only be interpreted as meaning that we on this side of the House are bigots. I did not like that. Now, in June of 1973, we have heard the comment of that noble gentleman, that noble Liberal, that noble person, Mr. Jack Pickersgill. He created his own job for retirement, left his $37,000 cabinet post for his $50,000 self-created job, and as soon as he got out decided he was going to be a Liberal again and called all of us Tories bigots. If you define bigotry as not understanding or not wanting to understand another person's point of view, then it follows that he who calls a person a bigot is a bigot himself.
To my way of thinking it is unfortunate that the government of today and the Liberal party seem to have cornered the market on calling people bigots. Let us do away with that word. Let us throw it out of parliament. That word should be tossed on the trash heap before the word "liar". It is easy to prove somebody a liar, but you cannot prove somebody a bigot because bigotry is a state of mind.
I am also sad because although the government says it feels this question is important and is a matter of priority,
June 5, 1973

the Prime Minister did not feel it was important enough, nor did the majority of his senior cabinet officials-especially those from Quebec-feel it was important enough to stick around in this chamber and hear other points of view. They did not even have the courtesy to hear the points of view presented by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and by the leaders of the other parties. That is some sense of priority, some sense of wanting to understand!
Any segment of society, whether it be French, English, East European, West European, Eskimo, Indian or what-have-you, is entitled to a sense of security. I will always vote for and support that which helps give a segment of people a sense of security if it does not encroach upon other people's sense of security. I said much the same thing in the recent debate on capital punishment. I say French-speaking Canadian felt threatened, felt that their sense of security was in jeopardy; therefore, to help provide them with a sense of security parliament deemed fit to enact the Official Languages Act. I support that act.
Now we have some unilingual, English-speaking Canadians who want the same feeling of security, and we have this resolution. The resolution is not much, but it is a small token in giving that sense of security and therefore I will gladly support it. However, I repeat that this resolution does not go far enough. If legislation was necessary to bolster the sense of security of French-speaking Canadians, then surely legislation is necessary to bolster the sense of security of English-speaking Canadians.
The resolution itself means nothing. It is not binding as a legal precedent. It cannot be pleaded in the courts. It cannot be cited in any court in this land. It has the same effect as Pearson's pledge, which has been referred to in this debate and which Mr. Carson said did not bind him at all; he said he went by the law of the land. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has already told this House that a resolution does not bind the government. Therefore, the government will not be bound by this resolution.
Through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) the government says that it wants to remain flexible. If it wants to remain flexible it must already have in mind the idea of changing these principles. I do not think they should be so flexible as to be changed at the whim of the government. There is no guarantee, as the Minister of Finance indicated yesterday, in this resolution for our civil servants. Claude Edwards, the leader of a group of public service employees, says he wants the resolution made into law, but not yet. Has Claude Edwards negotiated a contract, a collective agreement with the government? If he has, that does give those civil servants a sense of security because they can sue on the basis of a contract or collective agreement. But if he has not negotiated and signed such a collective agreement or contract, then members of the public service are being sold short by their leader in this instance: they have no security whatever.
I accept the principles contained in this resolution, but I ask the House to have the courage of its convictions and put those principles into law. If this amendment is defeated, if the members of the NDP let down the workers in the civil service, then their principles, the socialist principles of protecting employees, are once again swept under the
Official Languages
carpet and the English-speaking public servant is left with only hopes of good faith to depend on, with no law, no contract, no collective agreement. With this government, Mr. Speaker, I would never want to depend on its good faith.
If you have a contract or collective agreement, it can always be amended. It could be amended within minutes, with a notarial seal on it and a few signatures. If you have a law, it may take an amendment three or four days at the most to pass through the House of Commons. Surely that would give flexibility enough, if the government wants flexibility, and would provide security if a person wanted to go to court.
The Minister of Finance says it is a guarantee. It is a worthless guarantee. Perhaps we in this House should some time consider legislation dealing with guarantees, with unscrupulous salesmen delivering goods under a worthless guarantee. The only way to guarantee these principles is by contract, collective agreement of legislation. I can only add that if there is a contract or collective agreement stating these principles, then there is no need for this debate. If there is not an agreement, then we as good parliamentarians should make the resolution into law. This resolution is not being made into law. I believe it is only here to cause mischief-the old divide and rule principle. It is politically motivated. God, please don't divide my country over politics. The people of Canada are not causing disunity; it is the politicians in this chamber and the politicians outside this chamber, the ones who are hungering for power or who are trying to cling to power who are trying to divide this country for their own political ends.
Mr. Speaker, I did not come here to take part in the partitioning or dismembering of this country. Canada is too important and should not be pulled apart by politicians crying "unity", "bigotry", or "disunity". All politicians who make Canadian unity part of a partisan political process should be condemned. Even when the politicians are acting irresponsibly, as I believe we are in this debate, I plead with the members of the press to act responsibly. Don't use national unity, Canadian unity, for sensationalized stories. If the politicians are acting like children trying to pull Canada apart, I beg the press to condemn the politicians and to act to keep Canada together.
If the amendment to put the resolution into law in the near future is defeated, nevertheless, as I have already said, I will support the main motion. It really will be the case that if I cannot get a whole loaf, at least I might get a crumb. It will be negligible, perhaps a small deposit. I would not condemn those who choose to vote against the motion if the amendment is defeated, for they may be saying that if you give French-speaking Canadians a sense of security by putting the principle into law, you should also give English-speaking Canadians the same sense of security by putting it into law. What is good for the goose is good for the gander.
