subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry my colleagues are not clapping any louder.
Mr. Speaker, I was anxious, like so many others, to take part in this debate, and particularly as a Quebecer. I believe this is a very special opportunity to express, as a Quebecer and as a francophone, my opinions on the past which I will not describe because time does not allow me.
Still, I should like to make a few comments on the resolution and on the amendment under study. In 1970, we passed an official languages act that was very promising, and which I supported off-hand; I was very happy to do it. We hoped that, with this 1970 bill, we would eliminate the disappointment of some of the French-speaking people in this country and also, at the same time, ensure the security of the employees in the Civil Service.
I am not exaggerating when I say that the objectives sought or set at the time have not all been reached. Should we blame the government for this delay in the implementation of bilingualism throughout the Civil Service?
I would be tempted instead to blame a few responsible persons in the Civil Service, persons who may not have understood. There were certainly people within the public service who did not want to understand. One thing is certain: the government, that was supported by the great majority in Parliament, is also disappointed for having to give a date for the implementation of. the Official Languages Act within the Civil Service.
I said earlier, as a Quebecer, that I was very honoured to take part in this debate because I think this is a very special opportunity for any member to speak favourably not only on the great principle that bilingualism would be for the country but also on the implementation of this bilingualism.
History forces us to react when such a serious question is being discussed. I will not go so far as to say that the integral implementation of the government's resolution will achieve national unity.
To achieve national unity would require much more than the adoption of a resolution to be implemented as law; this is one aspect, among many others, that should be studied as soon as possible, that Canadians in general be led to believe in this implementation of bilingualism within the public service.
I have listened to several speeches and I quite appreciated the presentation of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The principles included in his resolution are suggestions

which will be workable to the extent where officials in the public service will make them workable.
I hope that thanks to this debate we will succeed in sensitizing, first those officials, and also all the hon. members to the importance of total implementation of bilingualism in the public service.
I will not go so far as to suggest that discussing the official languages in parliament could incite all Canadians to speak two languages. To give such a guarantee would be to mislead those who listen to us. But it is absolutely imperative that, within the federal institutions,-and I think that all hon. members will agree with me-every Canadian may be taken care of in one of our official languages, and that from sea to sea. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said, and I quote:
For almost a century, many French-speaking Canadians have been thinking: "The government in Ottawa is not our government ... it does not even speak our language". That is the kind of frustration which facilitated separatism.
I think that the Prime Minister was perfectly right in making that statement. Of course, more than an official languages act will be necessary to convince the Quebecers that the best and most beautiful place is still Canada. I will come back to that point anyway, Mr. Speaker.
I would also like to congratulate the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who first supported the resolution now before us and then for reasons that I greatly respect suggested that these suggestions should be incorporated into the Official Languages Act. I think that we must consider seriously the possible application of these proposals. Of course, the experience of the last three years leads us to be pessimistic, even though I am sure of the Prime Minister's good faith with regard to his goal, that is to say bilingualism within the public service. I am convinced of the Prime Minister's good faith as I am convinced of that of the Leader of the Official Opposition when he brings forward an amendment and says that he would like to see these proposals incorporated into the Official Languages Act, so that the delay of the last three years does not occur again.
Therefore, after thinking seriously about it, I am ready to support these proposals, though they are not perfect. However, I think that they deserve my consideration and confidence and I believe that the amendment before us deserves enough consideration to encourage me to support it, in order to facilitate the fastest and most complete application of these proposals. Should this amendment not get the support of the majority, I will do like so many others: I will gladly support the proposals submitted to us.
However, when we read some of the speeches again, we find that there are still weaknesses.
I also listened carefully to the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) who did not hesitate to support these resolutions and, as did the leader of the official opposition, mentioned the respect that those two party leaders have for French-speaking citizens of this country and the importance they attach to them. I think it is only fair to say that they showed their respect and consideration for that group which lives for the greater part in the
June 5, 1973

province of Quebec, and they proved their respect for that group on several occasions.
As to my honourable friends of the social credit party of Canada, I do not know what their position is and whether they are free to vote for or against the resolution. Judging from what the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) said, I would think it difficult for them to support that resolution. If I were more convinced that their amendment could be implemented, I would probably think more about it, but I have great doubts that the amendment moved by the social credit would be the solution.
I am told by a colleague that I cannot vote three ways. That is not my habit. However, I like to express my views and I may be in the best position to give credit to those who deserve it because I know that it is not always easy to congratulate an opponent and say publicly what is good and what is bad. I am free, Mr. Speaker, to appreciate and consider the fine comments which we have heard in this House.
I would also like to recall the hon. members the statistics which the member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) mentioned when he stated that in 1971, among the 66,675 positions to be filled by the public service in federal departments, only 8 per cent required a unilingual Frenchspeaking incumbent, while 80 per cent, that is ten times more, required only English. However, in 1972, contrary to the recommendations of the Dion report, only 12 per cent of senior employees were French-speaking and only half of them were from Quebec.
Therefore, the data given by the member for Saint-Hyacinthe give food for thought. They show how important it is not only to discuss the principles but especially to implement them as soon as possible. We have experienced failure in the past three years, although there has been some progress. This progress has been unsatisfactory, but it is clearly apparent that through legislation we could have greater success and better results.
I agree with some members, but perhaps I do not endorse the entire speech made by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). He said, for example, that he proposed the establishment of a royal commission. When the royal commission was suggested, he stated that he objected to it, under the circumstances and that the royal commission which cost $10 million has rather served to divide the country. I disagree with the right hon. member for Prince Albert. I have disagreed with him before and I still do because I think that although that inquiry cost $10 million and did not succeed in achieving national unity, it still had some good points: it has shown the Canadian entity with its qualities and defects. Any unbiased and sensible individual would admit that this inquiry opened our eyes to the current situation and we have every reason, by seriously analyzing the report, for correcting the shortcomings and injustice which do exist.
Mr. Speaker, if we want to respond to the desires of most Canadians we should respond unanimously if possible on a matter of principles put before us with a view to improving bilingualism within the public service. Several hon. members have urged their colleagues to show good will and objectivity.
Official Languages
I also heard some hon. members express certain fears on the part of English-speaking people about the proposals on official languages accepted three years ago. I think I can say that for us, French-speaking people, those fears are far behind us because we have known frustration; many French-speaking people have grown discouraged by slow progress and the impossibility of participating in the administration of this country.
Some are concerned and surprised to see that, particularly in the province of Quebec, people have given up on federalism. If you assess the results of the last hundred years, you will understand this discouragement; if I were to limit myself to the results of the last hundred years, I would certainly hesitate to remain in this House. However, efforts have been made for the last ten years. Some injustices have been alleviated and if you assess the results of the last ten years there is reason to be optimistic rather than pessimistic. Does one have to forget a long part of Canadian life?
The right hon. member for Prince Albert mentioned that he introduced in Parliament a measure to provide Canadians with bilingual cheques, with simultaneous translation, that he took steps to have certain French-speaking people apoointed to important posts; I think that, in all equity, we must recognize that on those occasions he did consider francophones. Mr. Speaker, one should not delude oneself and believe that those nominations or the bilingual cheques are adequate reasons to make francophones think that equality exists in this country.
We may very well talk about national unity, but woe unto him who thinks that the Official Languages Act is the only means to realize national unity! I for one prefer talking about national harmony.
Will we have to recognize that there are different regions having different needs? It is recognized in the House. I often hear hon. members talking about notable differences on a national basis. Of course some are reluctant to repeat that there exist two founding people, i am not afraid to say it, Mr. Speaker, because this is how I learned the Canadian history.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert mentioned that Confederation is the result of the association of English-and French-speaking people who believed that the destiny of the northern half of this continent could be fulfilled in unity, but not in uniformity, and I quite agree. Without the basic agreements expressed in British North America Act section 133 which ratify the rights pertaining to our country's languages, as well as in sections 91 and 92 stipulating that the provinces have jurisdiction over education and culture, Canada would never have been.
I do not believe it exaggerated to say that there are in Canada two founding nations. Naturally there is also, and I am delighted about it, the contribution of thousands of immigrants from various origin who deserve the respect of all Canadians, for they have contributed to the unification of Canada. But, just the same, how can we forget our origins and the true history of this country? Hence the need and the importance to recognize two official languages in this country.
4470

June 5, 1973
Official Languages
Now I believe that this opportunity is most important, for it allows us to ask hon. members to respect that goal which we must pursue. That is one aspect of the problems we are facing in this country. Its achievement will be possible to the extent that those responsible in the civil service will think like most members, for I am convinced that the majority of members will support the initial resolution.
In any event we must at least-and I dare hope so- support unanimously the proposals that are now before us. It is not a life insurance, of course; I think it is a minimum which is worth considering. We will have to control the implementation of these principles, within the time limits stated, in respect of some positions to be created. It is a way of proving to the anglophones and francophones that Parliament, since we can all discuss this matter, is making a real effort to correct some injustices. The word is not too strong, and several members have said so before me. There have been injustices, and it seems that the majority, in Parliament, want to correct them. I think that we must make an effort to reach this goal; others before me appealed to unity and the influence that unanimity could exercise in Parliament. But we still have to convince the responsible people and to control closely the integral implementation of the principles involved. If, unhappily, we do not get better results than we have had in the last three years, we will have to admit that the Leader of the Official Opposition is quite right in asking as he does in his amendment that these principles be included in the Official Languages Act.
So I dare hope that the speeches made in this House will finally convince us of the importance of this debate. I would like to say before I conclude my remarks that we must not let ourselves be fooled into believing that with the Official Languages Act we have succeeded in satisfying the French-speaking group.
Should anybody think that those proposals were introduced only for those people living in the province of Quebec, it would be a serious mistake. I think that we can achieve that national harmony, that is the understanding of all ethnic groups in this country, through legislation a lot more important than the Official Languages Act. These amendments concern the economy of Canada.
I read today in a Montreal newspaper that Mr. Gerard Filion, a man well known in the province of Quebec, dealt with economic separatism 30 years ago because already at that time Quebec milk producers were adversely affected by the feed grain policy which still creates problems today.
There is this language problem for French-speaking people, but there are also economic problems. I am also thinking about the attitude of Quebec authorities.
Earlier, I heard a colleague from the New Democratic Party talk about the late Maurice Duplessis. Heaven knows if he is known in Quebec! But, Mr. Speaker, attempts were made to blame him for a certain conservatism, or a refusal to approve federal policies at one time. The attitude of Quebec governments for the last 30 years has always been aimed at a decentralized federalism. That has not changed today and the premier is asking that certain powers be handed back.

That is how national harmony will be achieved in this country, namely through the recognition of Quebec's needs.
I admit that in other areas or other provinces in this country people do not think as we do and do not speak our language, but the citizens in those areas have the right to live as much as we have.
Therefore, if we all recognized the distinct differences between the various areas in this country, we would accept them and would come to understand them, while promoting for certain areas, certain jurisdictions that would not be the same in other areas, because needs are different.
Therefore, Quebec's position is clear enough on that point. It is the whole history of the province and its mentality that want that, and I believe nobody has the right to put obstacles in the way of the one who wishes to preserve such basic rights.
However, it is not only a question of language here, but of needs and a question of mentality, that mentality we would like to be recognized throughout this country, as Quebecers. We already recognize different mentalities and accept them.
Now I believe it is with objectives such as those that we shall achieve that national harmony for the good of all Canadians. I hope there will be unanimity at least in this House on the principle of bilingualism, which is a basic principle and an obviously necessary one, so that we may really prove that we are members of parliament of this day and age.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with full realization of the significance and importance of the subject that I rise to take part in this debate, a debate which has included eloquent speeches by members from all parties. It is obvious that bilingualism is a subject that concerns us all.
Some Canadians see the Official Languages Act, and the nine principles for implementing bilingualism in the public service, as necessary and long overdue steps by the government to formally acknowledge the French fact in Canada. Others see the act as an arbitrary, inequitable and poorly administered program which is neither feasible nor workable. This latter group appears to include the majority of English-speaking Canadians, very few of whom harbour any ingrained biases or prejudices against their French-speaking countrymen as has been suggested. I include myself within this group of Canadians who are unhappy with the government's philosophy of bilingualism as articulated in the Official Languages Act. To us, the act has done little but foster misunderstanding and divisiveness between English- and French-speaking Canadians. This is the tragedy of the Official Languages Act.
Rather than re-evaluating the entire act in the hope of arriving at solutions more satisfactory to all Canadians, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is asking parliament to confirm the basic principles of the government's program for bilingualism in the public service. What this means is simply that the government is asking parliament to tell them to do what they intend to do anyway, that is, carry out the nine-point policy. It is a farce so far as public
June 5, 1973

policy goes. The resolution has no value for it merely reiterates present government policy, and it will have no real effect upon the issue itself since it is not an enactment of legislation but an expression of opinion. It is evident that the Prime Minister's intention for this debate was not to enter into a constructive dialogue on bilingualism. Rather, as he himself said, his intention was to make it difficult for some members to hold ambiguous positions on bilingualism.
My position is unequivocal. While I recognize the obvious right of every French-speaking Canadian to deal with the federal government in French, and while I recognize the undeniable right of every French-speaking Canadian to have equal employment opportunities within the federal civil service, I do not recognize nor approve of the manner in which the government is going about guaranteeing these rights. I disagree with the way the Official Languages Act is being implemented. However, it is not the implementation of the act that is necessarily responsible for its disastrous results; it is the act itself. The Official Languages Act must be rewritten.
Four years have elapsed since the Official Languages Act was passed in parliament with an overwhelming majority. The act, which was thought by most members to be a logical and extremely necessary piece of legislation, has in practice proven to be just the opposite. The past four years have ushered in a new era, one of unprecedented misunderstanding between Canada's two founding peoples. This misunderstanding manifested itself clearly in the last election. There was a blacklash, and this blacklash will not be curbed until legislation is enacted which is both more fair and rational than that which we currently have before us. This does not mean arbitrary and binding regulations and stipulations. What it does mean is flexibility. It means taking account of the French fact in the public service, but only in direct proportion to their statistical numbers in the population, and vice versa for districts in which English-speaking persons are in the minority.
One example of the arbitrariness and rigidity which is characteristic of the Official Languages Act, and which does little to foster national unity, is the 10 per cent minority population rule used in drawing the boundaries for bilingual districts. In these districts bilingual government services are to be statutorily required rather than left to administrative judgments of significant demand and feasibility as otherwise ordered in the Official Languages Act. But how are the lines on the maps to be drawn?
The Canadian population is relatively mobile and, as the 1971 census has shown, French-English proportions change significantly over a decade. Are the boundaries of these districts to be redrawn every ten years? If so, we can be sure that such a move would cause much bitterness and irritation among the persons affected. The concept of bilingual districts must be abandoned. Instead, the government should rely on criteria of significant demand and feasibility to determine where bilingual government services should be provided. Such a move would do away with the ridiculous intention of the government to set up a surfeit of federally-declared bilingual districts, staffed
Official Languages
with persons having to satisfy inflexible bilingual criteria, in provinces where it is neither necessary not proportionately justifiable with regard to population.
It appears, however, that the government has no plans to change the policy and thereby move to allay the fears of those most affected. Such lack of understanding and action epitomizes exactly what is wrong with both the government and the Official Languages Act. Even the Commissioner of Official Languages, Mr. Keith Spicer, has suggested that the government take a second look at the idea of bilingual districts. The government's apparent refusal thus far to acknowledge Mr. Spicer's concern regarding bilingual districts is not surprising. The commissioner's frequent outbursts and sardonic humour have done nothing but further compound and intensify animosities between English- and French-speaking Canadians.
Why the Prime Minister has refrained from reprimanding the commissioner for his outlandish statements is anyone's guess. However, I suspect the Prime Minister of being somewhat sympathetic to the commissioner. After all, what the Prime Minister is attempting to achieve in this plastic debate is a distinctly measurable degree of divisiveness in this country on the entire subject of bilingualism. It is the Prime Minister's hope that from such divisiveness will emerge a feeling among many Canadians that he, and he alone, is Canada's last real hope for national unity-a sort of omniscient father called upon to bring together all his children.
It is obvious that the Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) believes this, having accused several of my Conservative friends of persecuting French Canadians. Statements like these from an avowed federalist are inexcusable and reprehensible and further compound the problem. As long as bias and prejudice are continually rekindled, they will continue to exist; and no legislation, least of all the Official Languages Act, will make things any different. But to rewrite the act would at least be a start at nurturing a new feeling of understanding and equality among Canada's two founding peoples.
In any revision of the act, several important problem areas, all of which have blatently manifested themselves in the public service over the past four years, would have to be examined. As I mentioned earlier, the premise upon which a new act must be established is one of services and opportunity based on numbers. Minority group representation in the federal civil service should be based upon their statistical numbers in the population. Similarly, bilingual districts as such must be scrapped. If there are 50,000 French-speaking Canadians in an English-speaking province, there should only be a proportionate number of French-speaking public servants to deal with them. Current quotas are arbitrary and unfair. For example, there is little logic in a regulation stipulating that 50 per cent of the administrative staff in the Winnipeg Manpower Office must be bilingual by 1978, when the amount of government business they carry on with French-speaking Manitobans hardly makes the rule justifiable.
Other quotas, such as those involving the defence department, which stipulate that 28 per cent of all officers in the Canadian armed forces must be French-speaking, are similarly ridiculous. Quotas such as this smack of

June 5, 1973
Official Languages
tokenism, and the possibility exists of some positions being filled with personnel merely because they are able to speak French.
The Official Languages Act also failed to take cognizance of the fact that learning another language is not always easy. Many public servants find it immensely difficult to master a new language and, as a result may be effectively prevented from moving into higher positions. Even those who are able to learn a new language with relative ease have problems with retention. This situation is exacerbated by the manner in which the public service has structured its French language training programs. Language specialists tell us that a person who studies a new language intensively for six weeks and then goes back to a job for the same period of time where that language is used only sparingly, can easily forget what he learned. Today this is a common occurrence in the Canadian public service, and an unnecessary one. The number of civil servants having to take part in these courses is totally out of proportion to the number that need to, or ever will, actually conduct their business in French.
Then there is the eroding effect that bilingualism has had on morale within the public service, not only in the national capital region where the results of October 30 indicate this widespread disaffection but throughout the country. Low employee morale is hardly conducive to good government. But perhaps the most serious concomitant effect of the entire bilingualism program has been the fantastic expenditure. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent by the government in implementing the federal bilingualism development program. The great portion of this money has been unnecessarily spent. The return on the investment has been poor.
One government practice in particular clearly illustrates to what I allude. I refer to the government's insistence that all government documents, books and pamphlets be printed and bound in both English and French. I am not arguing that inasmuch as both are official languages there should not be an English version and a French version of government publications, but why insist on having both versions within the one cover when only half will be used by the reader depending upon whether he speaks English or French? Even the Liberal Winnipeg Free Press pointed out that which is obvious when it said:
Government documents are twice as large as they need be and therefore twice as costly. English-speaking Canadians will not use that half of a publication that is written in French; nor will French-speaking Canadians use the English half. Why, then, does the government print and make the public buy both versions?
Then there is the question of language training. As many speakers have said before me, more money must be spent in promoting French language instruction in our schools, particularly our elementary schools. This is where learning begins, where language training can be most effective and where understanding of different cultures and people initially develops. But while more of our young people could be studying French, they are not. A recent study by the Ontario Department of Education shows that the number of students studying French in the province is declining rather than increasing. This decline is indicative of the dissatisfaction felt by many Canadians with regard to the Official Languages Act. The number of students

learning French is also declining in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
I could go on at some length reciting numerous other reasons why I am unhappy with the Official Languages Act and why I shall vote against this resolution. However, I think that my remarks sufficiently explain my position, one which is similar to that held by a great many Canadians, including the great majority of my constituents. I was thus astounded to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) who recently assured the House that bilingualism is highly supported and is received with great enthusiasm by all cultural groups in this country. I question his judgment and am anxious to know the name of the country to which he referred.
The Official Languages Act and the question of its legality is currently before the courts. Its principles are before parliament and will eventually be before the Canadian people in an election. The controversy, hostility and misunderstanding surrounding bilingualism will continue until a more satisfactory approach is sought and found. A fair and equitable solution to the problem can only be arrived at through further dialogue and with the adoption of more flexible legislation. Such a solution must also acknowledge to a much greater extent other cultures and languages. Then, and only then, will Canada be on the road toward achieving our elusive dream-that of national unity.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to congratulate the government on introducing this resolution. It is something they dreamed up following a great deal of consideration. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), being a very cunning man and somewhat repentant, so it appears, felt it was necessary to show the country that the government had had a change of heart. I think that is really the purpose of this resolution, to leave the country with the impression that the Liberal party is adopting a new line of thinking and that the Prime Minister has learned something from the election of October 30.
However, I want also to state that this resolution, in terms of today's news events, is Canada's answer to the United States' Watergate. This is the biggest cover-up we have ever experienced by a government that knows full well that it does not mean one word of what it is saying in this resolution. This resolution is an attempt to deceive the Canadian people.
Just what is a resolution, Mr. Speaker? I have attended a great many conventions in my day, and I am sure each member of this House has attended convention after convention in one capacity or another. What is a resolution? It is simply a recommendation to a higher authority. So what do we have here? We have the government in power, which is one authority introducing in the House of Commons, which is the final authority, a recommendation to itself: it is saying, "We recommend to ourselves that we do this".
If the Prime Minister and his government were sincere they would not try to deceive the people of Canada. But someone in this House of Commons has been able to call their bluff. I am not going to stand here, as a member of
June 5, 1973

this party or of any other party in this House, and have that kind of deceit, that kind of bluff, pulled on me. I do not think the Canadian people expect this sort of thing. If the Prime Minister or his cabinet were sincere today they would have introduced an amendment to the Officials Languages Act. That would have meant something. Certainly I would support that sort of amendment. Had the Prime Minister and the Liberal party done that, they would have called my bluff. Members who were here in the previous parliament will recall that I voted against the Official Languages Act. This act is now part of history. Obviously there is a feeling against it in certain parts of the country, contrary to the kind of hypocrisy that has existed in other parts.
In this chamber we have two standards. You can say things against English-speaking parts of Canada but you dare not say anything about French-speaking Canadians. You can say whatever you like about the other ethnic groups in this country. For example, what is happening in St. Boniface? The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) has been very vocal on many occasions, but what is happening to the radio station there? This radio station has provided Jews, Ukrainians and other ethnic groups with the chance to sing songs in their own language, but it is now being taken over by French-speaking Canadians.

subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO ALLEVIATE PROBLEMS CAUSED BY GREY SEALS IN CERTAIN AREAS OF ATLANTIC
FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO ALLEVIATE PROBLEMS CAUSED BY GREY SEALS IN CERTAIN AREAS OF ATLANTIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 29, as recorded at page 4209 of Hansard, I had occasion to ask the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), in charge of fisheries, a question with reference to the detrimental effect grey seals are having on certain fishing operations off the eastern shore of Nova Scotia. There is a real problem in this particular part of Atlantic Canada which is symbolic of the situation in other parts of Canada.
The whole inshore fishing industry is not getting the advantage it deserves, and it is under severe pressure. Anyone who has attended the proceedings of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, or has read the minutes of that committee knows that in

many respects the fishermen of eastern Canada are being short-changed. They are being short-changed in dredging, wharf repair and construction, breakwater maintenance, and so on. These aggravated problems are made worse in this particular area of my constituency and, incidentally, the constituency of the government House leader (Mr. MacEachen), by the activity of the grey seals.
The warden of the municipality of the district of St. Mary's, Howard Turner, who has been active in the fishing industry for many years, told me a few days ago that at one time he and others used to keep these animals in check and received bounty money for their trouble. At that time the fishermen were protected and the grey seals were kept in check. Now the situation is unfortunately reversed. The attitude of the government toward these fishermen in general is deplorable. The Department of Fisheries must be restored to its rightful place under a minister, and not lumped together with another department with other responsibilities.
The annual report of the Fisheries Prices Support Board, a government publication, indicates a decline in Canadian fisheries production. The annual Statistical Review of the Canadian fisheries for 1972, published by Environment Canada, illustrates Canada's position in world fisheries as being pretty mediocre: we are behind Russia, we are behind Japan, we are behind Norway and the United States. In terms of volume and value of catch we are behind these four countries. I suggest this is because our fishermen are not getting the backing or the protection and consideration they deserve.
About a year ago, because of a certain amount of agitation from the fishing industry the Minister of the Environment and the government House leader came to the town of Larry's River along with assorted officials. We had a very successful meeting there in terms of the number in attendance. At that time many promises were made about dredging, better wharves, better guidance systems and harbours. I do not have time to list the number of promises made but I certainly do not need much time to enumerate the promises that were kept. The fishermen in my constituency realize they are not being fairly treated. I know that the minister and many of his departmental officials hardly know the difference between a hake and a haddock, a cod fin and a capelin.
Let me refer again to the question of the grey seal. Unless something is done to relieve the situation, the fishermen will, in defence of their livelihood, be forced into disposing of these animals in contravention of the law. This is something no one wants to see happen, but unless consideration is given to some of the problems inherent in the inshore fisheries of Nova Scotia it is likely to happen.
This may not be strictly relevant to the question I directed to the Minister of Fisheries, but perhaps he would use his influence with the minister in charge of the Unemployment Insurance Commission to change the regulations so that fishermen can get better protection, in terms of unemployment insurance benefits, than they now get because of gross discrimination in terms of UIC benefits.

subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR ACTION TO ALLEVIATE PROBLEMS CAUSED BY GREY SEALS IN CERTAIN AREAS OF ATLANTIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) made a
June 5, 1973

statement which implied that the fishermen are being ignored. If he had read one of the recent reports of the Science Council of Canada he would have noted, for example, that the money which the federal government is spending on research and development in fisheries is the highest by all odds, for any industry in this country.
Ten per cent of the equivalent of the total value of output of the industry at the processing plant is spent by the taxpayers of Canada on research and development in the industry. If we take the total budget of the fishery service, it is equivalent approximately to 20 per cent of the value of the output of the industry.
There is no industry in Canada that gets this kind of support from the taxpayers of this nation, and that money is spent substantially on the east coast. It is roughly three times that spent on the west coast. It is spent in proportion to the value of the output of the industry.
I mentioned the figure of 10 per cent which is spent on research and development in proportion to the gross value of the industry. In agriculture, forestry and other industries the figure is more like 1 per cent. So in terms of R and D support the fishery is being treated ten times as well as forestry or agriculture. The fishery has not done badly in spite of what the hon. member said. Canada is behind Japan, Norway, Russia and the United States today. It has been behind them for many many years, those countries, being long-distance fishing nations, fishing all over the world. Some of them with very large populations and concerned about protein shortages have always taken many more fish than Canadians with a relatively small population. We are more efficient but we take fewer fish.
The grey seal population on the east coast has been growing. It is now in the order of 30,000. We do have a controlled culling operation which is carried out annually under the direction of our scientists. However, the population has increased and the problem is increasing. They are taking large numbers of mackerel, cod, herring, and so on. Because the number of fish off our shores has been decreasing due to excessive fishing pressure, we have to take seals because their population is rising and the ecological balance has been upset. I can assure the hon. member and the fishermen in his area that we have the grey seal problem very much in mind and we are doing something about it.

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-ABORIGINAL RIGHTS-VALIDITY OF ROYAL PROCLAMATION OF 1763
INDIAN AFFAIRS-ABORIGINAL RIGHTS-VALIDITY OF ROYAL PROCLAMATION OF 1763
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the occasion for the question which I addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last May 8 on the matter of aboriginal rights arose from two separate but related events. One was the statement made to the committee on Indian affairs by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) on April 12, 1973, as recorded at page 1329 of the proceedings of the committee which reads:
The proclamation of 1763 I recognize as a valid document-It establishes on obligation for the Crown to negotiate with the natives before taking land from the Indians.
Adjournment Debate
The second event was a little later, when this House was in recess and the Prime Minister made certain public statements on television, and perhaps otherwise, among other things suggesting that the NDP was trying to rewrite history and accusing us of lack of concern for what some of the provincial governments of Canada are doing in this area. This was sufficient cause for me to ask the Prime Minister whether the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development when he was speaking before the committee was stating government policy or not. While there were certain procedural difficulties to the question as I posed it, that essentially was the question I asked and on which I would like information. The Prime Minister in his reply said it was "a very difficult legal question which I am not able to settle in any final way by any answer or, indeed, by a statement of policy."
When the Prime Minister of this country, in this day and age, was so vague about it, I felt the answer was far from being satisfactory and that I should pursue the matter further on an occasion such as this. The nub of the question that arises in my mind is why the Prime Minister continues to deal with this matter as an abstract legal question rather than as a basic human question involving basic human rights. That is the point of view from which I would like to see the question treated. Incidentally, I say at once, Mr. Speaker, that if we can get a real statement of policy, in depth from that point of view, from the government of Canada then so far as I am concerned I am quite prepared to play my part with any provincial government in this country, regardless of its political stripe, in having that government recognize its appropriate responsibility in the consideration of this matter. But until there is forthcoming from the Government of Canada a clear-cut statement of its policy, it ill behooves the Prime Minister or anyone else to criticize the position being taken in this context by provincial administrations.
There are a couple of points I would like to mention in the few minutes available to me. One arises out of the further statement by the minister on April 12 when, in reference to the B.C. land question, he said:
In the B.C. land question the judges did not agree, they split. Three judges said that the proclamation of 1763 did not apply to B.C. because B.C. was terra incognita in 1763.
My response to that is again to say, let us get it out of the legal context. The fact is, and the records indicate it, that whether or not this legally applied, certainly the first Governor and the Colonial Secretary in London at that time acted as if it did apply. The documentary evidence on that point is quite clear, if one looks afield one can pick up that kind of factual recognition almost anywhere.
I have in my hand a copy of a book just published, "Barkley Sound-A History of the Pacific Rim National Park Area," by R. Bruce Scott in which he tells something of the life and adventures of William Eddy Banfield, described as a government agent, trader, explorer, writer, ship's pilot and the first white settler in Barkley Sound. Mr. Banfield in his rather voluminous reports to the Colonial Secretary at Government House, Victoria, a man named W. A. G. Young, had many interesting things to say. Among them is one of his reports dated Ohiat, Barclay Sound, 23rd February, 1860, in which he wrote:
4476

June 5, 1973
Adjournment Debate
I mentioned to His Excellency when at Victoria that I had made a purchase of my place at Ohiat from the Chief. I was almost compelled to do so on my first coming among them; they were particularly anxious that I should purchase the ground on which I lived... saying that the Americans at Cape Flattery had all bought their ground from the Indians. I pleaded poverty, which was very evident to them, my stores being very limited ... But to save myself the daily annoyance of the creatures I at length bought it for two blankets and two shirts. In order to impress on them formality, I drew out a title deed and explained it to them, giving them a duplicate. I had no civilized witness, none being in the neighbourhood.
Then Mr. Banfield goes on to explain how he later moved to another spot and bought another place. Inflation had set in, for his second property cost "six blankets, some beans, molasses, etc." Again he drew out a title deed. The evidence is clear for anyone who want to see that de facto recognition was given at one time by governmental authorities, and that all we really need to do is interpret the context of the present documents on human rights in relation to the situation as it was recognized then.
Mr. Speaker, when I talk about documents I have in my hand some of the international covenants on human rights, among them the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights of the United Nations, and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. In the preamble to the covenant of the assembly the text reads as follows;
Recognizing that, in accordance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the ideal of free human beings enjoying civil and political freedom and freedom from fear and want can only be achieved if conditions are created whereby everyone may enjoy his civil and political rights, as well as his economic, social and cultural rights.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) because it is good that once in a while he is caught in the position of defending the government.
Of course we recognize Indian rights in this country, and of course we do that in British Columbia; and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that. When the decision of the Supreme Court was handed down a few months ago in the case of the Nishga people's council, the court was divided and the Indians came to me and asked me to go and see the British Columbia government, which happens to be of the same political stripe as the hon. member's party. I went, and said to the British Columbia government that the Indians from the Nass River were asking British Columbia to turn over to them the land that belongs to them according to the decision of the Supreme Court.
I expected the NDP government in British Columbia to agree and say it was part of the policy of their government and party to recognize those rights. Oh, they were surprised that I said that to them and asked that they recognize in general terms the Indian rights. That means that the B.C. government has to return to the federal government, for the benefit of Indians of the Nass River, those lands that immemoriably belong to the Indians there. I

was flabbergasted to realize that they were not keen to do that. When it was time to deliver the goods, they were not there. They said, "Write us a letter about it." I wrote two months ago asking them to live up to the decision of the Supreme Court and deliver the land to the Nass River Indians. I am still waiting for an answer. So I hope the hon. member who is so devoted to the cause of Indians will go to his friends in British Columbia and tell them to live up to the program of his own party.
When the land was cut off from the Indians after 1912 during the time of the McBride commission a lot of land was taken away from the Indians and used by the province as Crown land. So I am going to the B.C. government once in a while asking them to return those lands that were taken away by the provincial authorities, for the benefit of the provincial government, from the Indians.
I am still waiting for British Columbia to live up to the commitment they made to the Indians during the last provincial election campaign, because this is a clear case where the rights of the Indians have not been lived up to by the provincial government and perhaps by the then federal government. So if the hon. member wants to cry in this House he should spend one day more, perhaps one week, on Vancouver Island and drive south to Victoria and speak to the provincial government.
I said in committee, and I repeat it here, that after the decision of the Supreme Court it is very clear that the royal proclamation by King George III in 1763 imposes an obligation to settle the Indian claims in a certain fashion. That is exactly why we have already started negotiations with the Yukon Indians, to settle their claims. That is why I am starting to establish acceptable mechanisms in order to find ways to solve the problems of those Indians in British Columbia who have not signed treaties.
I hope the hon. member for Comox-Alberni will employ some energy and use his facility with language to explain this to his friends in British Columbia who do not seem to be ready to deliver what they have promised to the electorate of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, on May 9 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whether, in light of the fact that he had promised residents of the Toronto region that he would cancel the Pickering airport development if more than 51 per cent of the people in metro Toronto were opposed to it, he would treat a recent public opinion poll in the Toronto Star as indicative of the feelings of the people of the region, or would he prefer to treat the opinion of the NDP on this issue in view of their switch in position in committee, as indicative of public opinion. The Prime Minister refused to answer. The words I am about to refer to were uttered in the borough of Scarborough, but they would apply to the whole of metropolitan Toronto. They were spoken on March 25, 1972, and are as follows-that if the majority of people living in this area, even if only 51 per cent, did not want this airport, the government would not proceed with it.
June 5, 1973

There have always been a great many people in the Toronto region who have questioned the need for a second airport. It was a major issue, in the election campaign in the Toronto region, of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who went on record as early as September 30, 1972, as saying that the case for a second Toronto airport had not been made. Fourteen of the 22 successful candidates in the metro Toronto region who ran in the October 30 election were on record during the election campaign as saying that there was no proven need for a second airport. Yet still the government pushed ahead, convinced that the public was still behind them on this.
Then some of the municipal councils got into the act, namely, Toronto city council representing 700,000 people, the regional municipality of York representing 166,000 people, and the township of Pickering representing 30,000 people. The councils of all these municipalities expressed opposition to the airport proceeding as planned. Yet the government still persisted. Then the Swackhammer report was completed early in January of this year, indicating that there were weighty technical arguments against the airport proceeding. As well, there was further evidence of widespread public opposition. Yet the government charged blindly ahead and on January 30 confirmed the expropriation notices on some 18,000 acres of land even though there has not been an independent inquiry to allow full public participation on the question of the need and site of the location.
That was over four months ago, Mr. Speaker. We are still waiting for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to announce the terms of reference and membership of the independent inquiry, notwithstanding that he originally promised that it would be reporting within one year of his January 30 announcement. We are anxiously awaiting that announcement and I hope it will be made very shortly.
As for public opinion, there was further evidence brought to the attention of the government on April 28 of this year when the Toronto Star published the result of a poll carried out by Canadian Facts Company Ltd. during the first ten days of April. This poll was conducted on a number of national and local issues and included a sample of 407 eligible voters across metro Toronto. The poll concluded with this question: Are you in favour of the proposed new airport scheduled to be built in Pickering township, or are you against it?
The result in metropolitan Toronto was as follows: 56 per cent of the people were against the airport, only 26 per cent said they were in favour, and 18 per cent said they were not sure. In the city of Toronto, which contains the riding of St. Paul's which I represent, the result was as follows: 62 per cent were against the airport, 19 per cent were in favour of it, and 19 per cent were not sure. Mr. Adjournment Debate
Speaker, over three to one were against it in the city, and if you take the entire metropolitan region, over two to one were against the airport.
Is it not about time to say to the Prime Minister: How about it? Will you honour your word to the people of the metropolitan Toronto region? Will the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport continue to ignore the facts which I have stated, or will the government continue to push blindly ahead, bolstered by the votes in committee of NDP members who in a moment of utter hypocrisy voted on estimates to give the government the money to push ahead with this unnecessary project? The whole project at Pickering runs counter to the environmental, economic and human needs of the urban region of metropolitan Toronto. When will this government begin to listen to the people?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Atkey) I wish to say that the minister has clearly outlined his views at the committee level.
Projections indicate that by the end of the century, Toronto will have in excess of six million people. Toronto is the hub of our domestic air transportation system. Air travel is no longer for the wealthy few. Air cargo will be a vital part of our future economic activities. Many times more facilities than those we have now will be required. In 1968 we abandoned the idea of expanding Malton airport due to the threat of noise and due to the surrounding development. Malton's traffic will be further expanded, but not its size. Even considering the quieter aircraft we will have in the future, Malton would have too many flights, considerable noise problems and too high a volume of aircraft unless the airport is enlarged. A new airport is required.
The Ontario government has a plan for regional development known as the Toronto centred region and we have been able to achieve a consensus of view with the Ontario government in selecting a new site consistent with their planning. Pickering meets aviation criteria, is convenient and can be developed to meet future demand. Those persons owning on land expropriated will be paid not only the market value but also related payments for relocation and disturbance. Also, a great deal of expropriated land can be made available for agricultural use within the airport zone.
Hearings under the Expropriation Act have been held. Everyone has been given time to be heard; yet no one need be disturbed nor will construction begin until a board of examination, working with the three levels of government concerned, determines the type and timing of facilities required.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10:30 p.m.
